structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Document type and placement: RBI Group’s consolidated non-financial statement for financial year 2024, included for the first time as a dedicated chapter within the 2024 annual financial report’s group management report (not a standalone report).
- Reporting framework and regulations: Prepared under the CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), Austrian Commercial Code (sections 267a, 243b) and NaDiVeG; structured in line with ESRS, using a double materiality assessment. Includes prescribed Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures as separately identifiable sections and adds selected elements requested by rating agencies and stakeholders.
- Scope and consolidation: Prepared on a consolidated group basis aligned with IFRS scope; key figures relate to the RBI Group unless stated otherwise. Coverage extends to upstream and downstream value chains, with references to the Scope of consolidation and Definition of value chain.
- Assurance and publication: Independently audited with limited assurance by Deloitte Audit Wirtschaftsprüfungs GmbH; published annually; 2024 statement released on 25 February 2025.
- Transparency choices: No exclusions for intellectual property/innovation-sensitive information; no omission of impending developments or matters under negotiation.
- Content structure and themes covered:
  - General information and Basis of preparation
  - Governance
  - Strategy related to sustainability
  - Impact, risk and opportunity management
  - Environmental information, including:
    - EU Taxonomy Article 8 regulatory disclosures
    - Climate change
    - Biodiversity and ecosystems
    - Resource use and circular economy
  - Social information, including:
    - Own workforce
    - Workers in the value chain
    - Affected communities
    - Consumers and end-users
  - Governance information:
    - Business conduct
    - Responsible banking progress statement for UN PRB signatories
- Purpose and audience: Addresses all RBI stakeholders, describing direct and indirect economic, environmental, and social impacts, related risks and opportunities, management approaches, and stakeholder considerations.

nodes.title: General basis for preparation of the consolidated non-financial statement
nodes.heading: BP-1: General b asis for preparation of the consolidated non-financial statement
nodes.start_phrase:
The consolidated non-financial statement provides information on RBI’s non-financial agenda s and activities for the reporting 
year 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and placement: Summarized consolidated non-financial statement (NFS) for RBI Group for reporting year 2024, included for the first time as a dedicated chapter within the 2024 annual financial report’s group management report (not a standalone report).
- Reporting frameworks and legal bases: Prepared under the CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), Austrian Commercial Code (sections 267a, 243b), NaDiVeG, and based on ESRS; includes Article 8 disclosures of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and related delegated acts as separately identifiable sections.
- Scope and boundaries: Prepared on a consolidated basis aligned with the financial consolidation perimeter under IFRS as adopted by the EU; covers upstream and downstream value chains; key figures relate to the RBI Group unless otherwise stated.
- Content focus: Reports on sustainability strategy; material economic, environmental, and social impacts identified via double materiality; related financial risks and opportunities and their management; consideration of stakeholder views; includes some additional disclosures requested by sustainability rating agencies and other stakeholders.
- Structure: Organized according to the ESRS disclosure framework.
- Audience and frequency: Addresses all RBI stakeholders; published annually.
- Publication and assurance: 2024 NFS released on 25 February 2025; independently audited with limited assurance by Deloitte Audit Wirtschaftsprüfungs GmbH.
- Transparency choices: No exclusions for intellectual property/know-how or innovation results; no omissions of impending developments or matters under negotiation.
- Cross-references: Further details on consolidation in “Scope of consolidation” and IFRS note (59) Group composition; value chain defined in the “Definition of value chain” chapter.

nodes.title: Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances
nodes.heading: BP-2: Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances
nodes.start_phrase:
For climate and environment-related risk, RBI differentiates between the impact expected in the short, medium and long term 
in line with the European Central Bank (ECB) guide on managing climate-related and environmental risks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on BP-2 disclosures covering climate- and environment-related risk management with ECB-aligned time horizons and a forward-looking approach beyond typical planning/loan tenors.
- Short term (0–3 years): Primarily transition risks from regulation and technology changes; opportunities to finance clients’ transition, green industries, and circular economy; observed increase in physical events (e.g., floods in CEE).
- Medium term (3–10 years): Combined transition and rising physical risks if decarbonization lags; risks from technological obsolescence and immature innovations; regulatory tightening potentially eroding profitability; investor exit from fossil fuels signaling asset devaluation (carbon bubble); opportunities in profitable new technologies and coal divestment.
- Long term (>10 years): Dominance of physical risks affecting customer business models, supply chains, and repayment capacity; disorderly transition scenarios imply significant losses, especially for carbon-intensive sectors.
- Estimation and outcome uncertainty: Value chain metrics often based on averages/assumptions; preference for client-reported data, with disclosure when not current; use of external/sector averages and multiple sources; expected uncertainty reduction via ESRS standardization; key estimated metric is financed Scope 3 emissions with PCAF-aligned data quality disclosures; high measurement uncertainty flagged where applicable.
- ESG customer score: Applied to corporates and project finance to assess ESG performance, mid- to long-term ESG-related risk, and to classify customers (restrictive/transformative/supportive) for underwriting decisions.

nodes.title: Time horizons
nodes.heading: Time horizons
nodes.start_phrase:
For climate and environment-related risk, RBI differentiates between the impact expected in the short, medium and long term 
in line with the European Central Bank (ECB) guide on managing climate-related and environmental risks.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines RBI’s climate and environmental risk disclosures, defining time horizons aligned with the ECB guide and adopting a forward-looking approach beyond typical planning and loan tenors.
- Short term (0–3 years): Emphasis on transition risks from regulatory and technological changes; opportunities to finance client transitions, renewables, and circular economy; acknowledgement of increasing physical risk events (e.g., floods).
- Medium term (3–10 years): Combined transition and physical risks; risks from technological obsolescence and immature innovations; heightened regulatory pressure; potential devaluation of fossil-related assets (carbon bubble); opportunities in profitable new technologies and coal divestment.
- Long term (>10 years): Predominantly physical risks impacting customer business models, supply chains, and repayment capacity; disorderly transition scenarios imply major losses, especially for carbon-intensive sectors.
- Estimation and outcome uncertainty: Sustainability data sought directly from clients; where unavailable, multiple external sources and sector averages are used; ESRS adoption is expected to reduce uncertainty. Key estimated metrics include scope 3 financed emissions with PCAF-aligned data quality disclosures; high measurement uncertainty is flagged where applicable.
- RBI has developed an ESG customer score for corporates and project finance to assess ESG performance, evaluate mid- to long-term ESG-related risks, classify customers (restrictive/transformative/supportive), and inform underwriting decisions.

nodes.title: Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty
nodes.heading: Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty
nodes.start_phrase: Quantitative information about key value chain activities is often based on averages, assumptions and estimates.
nodes.summary:
Summary of main points in the partial document:

- Purpose and framework: Describes RBI’s disclosures on specific circumstances (BP-2), explaining how climate and environmental risks are managed across distinct time horizons, aligned with the ECB guide. Because loan tenors are shorter than climate-risk realization periods, RBI applies a forward-looking, longer-than-usual horizon.

- Time horizons and risk/opportunity profile:
  - Short term (0–3 years): Predominantly transition risks from policy, regulation, and technology changes; opportunities in financing client transitions, renewables, and circular economy; early signs of rising physical risks (e.g., CEE floods).
  - Medium term (>3–10 years): Combined transition and physical risks; business model shifts, tech disruption, regulatory tightening; potential stranding of carbon-intensive assets (carbon bubble); risks from obsolete technologies or immature innovations; opportunities in profitable new technologies and divestment from coal.
  - Long term (>10 years): Physical risks dominate, affecting customers’ models, supply chains, and repayment capacity; scenarios indicate large losses, especially for carbon-intensive sectors if transition is disorderly.

- Estimation and uncertainty: Sustainability metrics often rely on averages, assumptions, and external/sector data when client data is unavailable; multiple sources are used. RBI expects uncertainty to decline with ESRS adoption. Scope 3 financed emissions are key metrics estimated, reported with data quality per PCAF 2022; high measurement uncertainty is flagged where relevant.

- ESG customer score: An internal scoring tool for corporates and project finance to assess ESG performance, gauge mid- to long-term ESG-related risks, categorize clients (restrictive, transformative, supportive), and inform underwriting decisions.

nodes.title: ESG customer score
nodes.heading: ESG customer score
nodes.start_phrase: The ESG customer score is used to:
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines RBI’s climate- and environment-related risk disclosures, focusing on time horizons, data uncertainties, and its ESG customer assessment framework.

- Time horizons for risk management (aligned with the ECB guide):
  - Short term (0–3 years): Predominantly transition risks (regulatory and technological change) with emerging physical risks; financing opportunities in supporting client transition, renewables, and circular economy.
  - Medium term (3–10 years): Business model shifts, rapid tech change, tightening regulation, rising physical risks if decarbonization lags; risks of stranded/outdated technologies, immature innovations, and regulatory impacts; investor retreat from fossil fuels (carbon bubble) versus opportunities in profitable new technologies and coal divestment.
  - Long term (10+ years): Dominance of physical risks affecting client business models, supply chains, and repayment capacity; scenario analyses point to large losses for carbon-intensive sectors under disorderly transition.

- Estimation and outcome uncertainty:
  - Sustainability metrics often rely on averages, assumptions, and multiple external data sources when client data are unavailable.
  - Anticipated reduction in uncertainty as ESRS adoption increases data availability and standardization.
  - Scope 3 financed emissions are a key metric estimated using indirect sources, disclosed with data quality per PCAF (2022), and flagged for high measurement uncertainty.

- ESG customer score:
  - Purpose: Assess customer ESG performance, mid- to long-term ESG-related risk, and categorize clients (restrictive/transformative/supportive) to inform underwriting.
  - Method: Internal analyst assessments combining quantitative and qualitative E, S, and G factors for all corporate credit customers; applied to corporate, project finance, and sovereigns; extended to financial institutions by end-2024.
  - Environmental: Evaluates transition and physical risks; focuses on net-zero alignment, circular economy, biodiversity; considers CO2 (Scopes 1–3), energy use, reduction targets, water use, renewables share, and qualitative environmental actions.
  - Social: Assesses social risks, compliance with health and human rights; enhanced human-rights module; reviews codes of conduct, supplier screening, workplace safety, business conduct, diversity/education; organized into general, human capital/human rights, responsible production, product-related, and customer-related aspects.
  - Governance: Reviews transparency, ethics, diversity, strategy, and risk management at top management level.

- Customer ESG data collection:
  - RBI deploys a standardized questionnaire emphasizing environmental data (S and G covered in existing ratings) to improve ESG scoring and financed emissions calculations.
  - In Austria, uses OeKB’s ESG Data Hub for a uniform, multi-bank questionnaire; promotes similar cooperation and harmonized national questionnaires in other markets.

nodes.title: Customer data collection
nodes.heading: Customer data collection
nodes.start_phrase:
ESG data availability is crucial for RBI to develop internal customer ESG scoring, improve the financed emissions and make 
informed internal steering decisions.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines RBI’s ESG customer scoring framework, covering Environmental (E), Social (S), and Governance (G) components and their use across corporate, project finance, and sovereign customers; rollout to financial institutions by year-end 2024.
- Environmental scoring assesses transition and physical climate risks, focusing on net-zero transition, circular economy, and biodiversity; combines quantitative metrics (e.g., Scope 1–3 emissions, energy and water use, reduction targets, renewables share) with qualitative assessment of actions to reduce footprint.
- Social scoring identifies customer-level social risks and positive impacts relative to RBI’s standards and reputation, with an enhanced focus on human rights; evaluates code of conduct and supplier screening, workplace safety, business conduct, diversity, and education.
- Social assessment is structured across five areas: general information; human capital/human rights; responsible production; product-related aspects; and customer-related aspects.
- Governance scoring examines transparency, business ethics, diversity, strategy, and risk management at top management level.
- ESG scores are determined via internal analyst assessments using both qualitative and quantitative data for all corporate credit customers.
- Describes ESG data collection strategy centered on an environmental questionnaire, while social and governance data are drawn from rating processes and public reports.
- In Austria, RBI uses OeKB’s ESG Data Hub to standardize questionnaires across banks; supports similar harmonized approaches in other markets, including national standards where applicable.
- The questionnaire covers key environmental topics: GHG emissions and reduction targets, circular economy, energy and water consumption, and EU Taxonomy KPIs (turnover, CapEx); examples of requested KPIs include Scope 1–3 emissions, taxonomy-eligible/aligned turnover shares, and renewable energy consumption share.
- Measures to improve ESG data availability and quality include client engagement and awareness, board-level KPIs, data quality checks, and progress dashboards.
- References related CSRD disclosures for Green Asset Ratio, financed emissions, and climate target setting in dedicated chapters.
- Notes RBI’s 2021 commitment to the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, aligning with the SDGs and the Paris Agreement, with progress reported in a dedicated chapter.
- Explains regulatory ESG risk disclosure under EBA’s Pillar 3 ITS (since 2022), with qualitative information aligned to ESRS in the non-financial statement and quantitative details available on RBI’s website.

nodes.title: Principles for Responsible Banking
nodes.heading: Principles for Responsible Banking
nodes.start_phrase:
In 2021, RBI became an official signatory of the Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB), and was the first Austrian banking 
group to do so.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of RBI’s ESG data collection: Uses RBI’s ESG questionnaire and OeKB’s ESG Data Hub to capture key environmental aspects (GHG emissions, reduction targets, circular economy, energy and water consumption, EU Taxonomy KPIs for turnover and CapEx).
- Sources and KPIs: Social and governance data drawn from annual and sustainability reports; requested KPIs include Scope 1–3 GHG emissions, share of taxonomy-eligible and -aligned turnover, and share of renewable energy consumption.
- Data quality and governance: Measures to enhance availability and quality include client engagement and awareness, board-level KPIs, data quality checks, and progress tracking via reports and dashboards.
- Linkages to CSRD: Additional Pillar 2 topics are detailed in specific CSRD chapters—Green Asset Ratio (Article 8 EU Taxonomy), financed emissions (E1-6), and climate target setting (E1-4).
- Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB): RBI became a PRB signatory in 2021, aligning banking activities with the UN SDGs and Paris Agreement under UNEP FI’s six principles; progress is reported in the Responsible banking progress statement for PRB signatories.
- Regulatory ESG risk disclosures: Compliance with EBA ITS on Pillar 3 ESG risk disclosures since FY 2022 to enhance transparency and comparability; qualitative information aligns with ESRS and is included in the consolidated non-financial statement, while quantitative Pillar 3 data is provided on RBI’s website with cross-references.

nodes.title: Regulatory disclosure of ESG risks
nodes.heading: Regulatory disclosure of ESG risks
nodes.start_phrase:
Since the 2022 financial year, it has been mandatory to disclose the Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) on Pillar 3 
disclosures on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks as published by the EBA.
nodes.summary:
- Describes RBI’s ESG data collection approach, using RBI’s ESG questionnaire and the OeKB ESG Data Hub to capture key environmental aspects (GHG emissions, reduction targets, circular economy, energy and water consumption, EU Taxonomy KPIs for turnover and CapEx).
- Sources social and governance information from annual and sustainability reports.
- Details requested KPIs from clients, including Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions; shares of taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned turnover; and share of renewable energy consumption.
- Outlines measures to enhance data availability and quality: client engagement and awareness, board-level KPIs, data quality checks, and progress visualization via reports and dashboards.
- Points to related CSRD/ESRS chapters for additional topics: Green Asset Ratio (EU Taxonomy Article 8), financed emissions (E1-6), and climate target setting (E1-4).
- Summarizes RBI’s commitment to the UN Principles for Responsible Banking, highlighting alignment with the SDGs and Paris Agreement and referencing a progress statement chapter on implementation.
- Explains regulatory ESG risk disclosure under EBA’s Pillar 3 ITS (mandatory since FY2022), aimed at improving transparency, comparability, and market discipline.
- Clarifies disclosure locations: qualitative information aligned with ESRS in the consolidated non-financial statement with cross-references from Pillar 3, while quantitative Pillar 3 metrics are available on RBI’s website.

nodes.title: Incorporation by reference
nodes.heading: Incorporation by reference
nodes.start_phrase:
Some ESRS disclosure requirements are closely linked to requirements that RBI is already subject to, such as the requirement in 
the Corporate Governance Code to describe its governance structure.
nodes.summary:
- Explains “incorporation by reference,” linking ESRS disclosure requirements to existing RBI reporting (Corporate Governance Code, consolidated financial statements, corporate governance report, group management report).
- Identifies phased‑in ESRS disclosures and where they are reported: E4‑6 (biodiversity and ecosystem financial effects) and E5‑6 (resource use and circular economy financial effects) in the Group management report.
- Outlines governance under ESRS GOV‑1, detailing the roles of the Management Board and Supervisory Board as the highest ESG decision-making bodies, with clear reporting lines and oversight of impacts, risks, and opportunities across RBI’s operations and value chain.
- Describes RBI’s Austrian dualistic board system, independence and suitability requirements, diversity and independence disclosures referenced to the Corporate Governance Report, and delineation of responsibilities via internal bylaws.
- Maps the sustainability governance framework: Supervisory Board committees (e.g., Risk, Audit, Remuneration, Nomination, Personnel, Digitalization), Management Board, and program/implementation structures (Sustainable Finance Group, ESG & Sustainability Management, Sustainability Committee, ESG Group Competence Center, Sustainable Bond & Deposit Committee, Environmental Committee, Sustainability Council, ESG business ambassadors, sustainability officers, responsible banking employees, cross‑functional task forces).
- Notes integration of sustainability strategies into performance management across board areas, with further details referenced to GOV‑2.
- Lists key external initiatives and memberships relevant to sustainability (e.g., AFRAC, Diversity Charters, EACB, Finance for Biodiversity, NZAM, PCAF, PRB, PRI, Raiffeisen Sustainability Initiative, respACT, SBTi, The Valuable 500, UNEP FI, UNGC, Vienna Initiative, VfU).

nodes.title: The role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.heading: GOV-1 : The role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.start_phrase:
Information about the reporting lines to the Management Board and Supervisory Board can be found in the table Governance 
of sustainability in RBI below.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines RBI’s governance structure for sustainability under Austria’s dualistic board system, with the Management Board and Supervisory Board as the highest decision-making bodies for ESG matters, collectively overseeing key impacts, risks, and opportunities across operations and the value chain.
- Clarifies independence and suitability requirements for board members in line with ESRS, delineation of responsibilities in bylaws, and embedding of sustainability strategies into performance management across board areas.
- Details Supervisory Board committee landscape relevant to ESG oversight: Working, Risk, Audit, Remuneration, Nomination, Personnel, and Digitalization committees.
- Describes Management Board–level ESG governance and cross-functional structures: Sustainable Finance Group, ESG & Sustainability Management, Sustainability Committee, ESG Group Competence Center, holistic ESG integration within Risk/Compliance/Finance/People, Sustainable Bond and Sustainable Deposit Committee, Environmental Committee (in-house ecology), and a Sustainability Council engaging internal and external stakeholders.
- Specifies implementation roles across the group: ESG business ambassadors in business units, sustainability officers in subsidiaries, responsible banking employees, and cross-functional task forces executing ESG measures.
- Lists key external memberships and initiatives supporting sustainability alignment and disclosure (e.g., AFRAC, Charta der Vielfalt, EACB WG on Sustainable Finance, Finance for Biodiversity, NZAM, PCAF, PRB, PRI, Raiffeisen Sustainability Initiative, respACT, SBTi, The Valuable 500, UNEP FI, UNGC, Vienna Initiative, VfU).
- Presents RBI’s Vision 2025 and mission, stakeholder commitments (customers, employees, shareholders, general public), and strategic pillars: sustained growth, customer centricity, efficiency, and speed/adaptability, with focus areas such as ESG integration, data-driven customer understanding, digitization/automation, cyber resilience, and People & Culture (talent, leadership, effective teams, learning, responsibility).
- Explains the Group Strategic Roadmap: a two-year, group-wide implementation tool cascading objectives from the Management Board to individual employees; ESG KPIs for Management Board members approved by the Personnel Committee and linked to remuneration; strategy accessible to all employees.
- Describes progress monitoring: quarterly reporting of strategic initiatives to the Management Board and Supervisory Board via an electronic system enabling timely responses to changing market conditions.
- Notes the sustainability expertise of both boards, reinforced by ongoing in-house and external training (including Fit & Proper), to effectively oversee material ESG topics (e.g., carbon footprint, human rights, governance), manage climate/compliance/reputational risks, and capture opportunities in sustainable investment and green finance.

nodes.title: Sustainability Council
nodes.heading: Sustai nability Council
nodes.start_phrase:
RBI’s Sustainability Council has become firmly established as a core organizational component of stakeholder dialogue and as 
part of sustainability management.
nodes.summary:
- Describes RBI’s ESG governance structure, focusing on the Sustainability Council and the Sustainability Committee, plus the Responsible Banking Task Force.
- Sustainability Council:
  - Established as a core element for stakeholder dialogue and sustainability management.
  - Comprised of external ESG experts and RBI decision-makers; chaired by RBI’s CEO.
  - Meets twice yearly; organized by Group ESG & Sustainability Management.
  - Advises on sustainability agenda development, materiality, target-setting, measures, and provides recommendations.
  - Lists internal and external members as of 31 December 2024.
- Sustainability Committee:
  - Cross-functional body supporting the Management Board’s ESG decisions; chaired by a Management Board member responsible for sustainable business (Marie-Valerie Brunner).
  - Composed of divisional heads with ESG focus; serves as advisory and recommendation body.
  - Ensures vigilance on ESG risks, supports sustainable business and projects, and advances a holistic sustainability approach.
  - In 2024 met nine times; prioritized business transformation, faster ESG data collection, integrating ESG into business practice, communication and stakeholder engagement, and regulatory compliance.
  - Responsibilities include:
    - Advising the Management Board on material ESG impacts, risks, and opportunities, including strategy and regulatory needs.
    - Recommending ESG KPIs for Management Board performance management at head office and subsidiaries.
    - Monitoring alignment with the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
    - Reviewing ESG strategy for Paris Agreement alignment and SDG commitments.
- Responsible Banking Task Force:
  - Mirrors the committee’s cross-functional composition; meets monthly.
  - Defines, coordinates, and consolidates key ESG topics and prepares agendas for the Sustainability Committee.

nodes.title: Sustainability Committee
nodes.heading: Sustainability Committee
nodes.start_phrase: The Management Board is supported in its ESG decisions by the cross-functional Sustainability Committee.
nodes.summary:
- RBI has a multi‑layer ESG governance structure centered on a Sustainability Council, a cross‑functional Sustainability Committee, a Responsible Banking Task Force, Group ESG & Sustainability Management under the CEO, the CFO area, and Group Internal Audit.
- Sustainability Council:
  - Established forum for stakeholder dialogue and sustainability management, composed of external ESG experts and RBI decision makers; chaired by the CEO.
  - Meets twice a year; organized by Group ESG & Sustainability Management.
  - Advises on sustainability agenda development, materiality focus areas, target setting, measures, and recommendations.
  - As of 31 December 2024, includes named internal and external members from management, academia, NGOs/foundations, and subsidiaries across the Group.
- Sustainability Committee:
  - Advisory and recommendation body to the Management Board on ESG; chaired by Management Board member Marie‑Valerie Brunner.
  - Comprised of divisional heads with ESG expertise; ensures vigilance on ESG risks, supports sustainable business/projects, and promotes a holistic ESG approach.
  - Met nine times in 2024, focusing on business transformation, accelerating ESG data collection, integrating ESG into business practice, communication and stakeholder engagement, and regulatory compliance.
  - Tasks include advising on material ESG impacts/risks/opportunities, recommending ESG KPIs for Management Board performance management, monitoring alignment with the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, and reviewing strategy for Paris alignment and SDG commitments.
- Responsible Banking Task Force:
  - Mirrors the Committee’s composition; meets monthly to define, coordinate, and compile key ESG issues and pre‑discuss Committee agendas, overseeing operational implementation.
- Group‑wide ESG coordination:
  - Top‑down and bottom‑up processes ensure involvement of all relevant functions and stakeholders.
  - ESG officers and ambassadors are appointed across subsidiaries to standardize and coordinate the Group’s approach.
- Group ESG & Sustainability Management (reporting to the CEO):
  - Acts as internal ESG advisor; plans, implements, and develops RBI’s ESG approach.
  - Works with business units and subsidiary sustainability officers across CEE and Austria; central point of contact and center of expertise.
  - Supports setting environmental and social targets and deriving improvement measures aligned with international standards.
  - Jointly with Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, manages proper annual non‑financial disclosures in the consolidated non‑financial statement; fulfills UNEP FI PRB commitments and engages with ESG rating agencies.
- CFO area:
  - Leads sustainability and management reporting for sustainable financing; ensures control, monitoring, data collection, budgeting, and reporting.
  - Sets policies and frameworks, integrates sustainability metrics into budgeting, and collaborates (e.g., with Sustainable Finance) to define targets for Corporates and Retail.
  - Co‑leads the consolidated non‑financial statement with Group ESG, ensuring accurate collection/analysis and integration of financial and ESG data.
- Group Internal Audit:
  - Independent, group‑wide, risk‑based audit function supporting the Management Board, Supervisory Board, and Audit Committee.
  - Steers local audit functions; maintains independence from decision‑making and business processes.
  - Ensures quality via ongoing monitoring, self‑assessments, and external quality assessments at least every five years, aligned with Global Internal Audit Standards.
  - Integrates ESG across audit planning and execution—via specific ESG audits or embedded topics—informing annual/quarterly plans; several audits in 2024 covered ESG topics.

nodes.title: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
nodes.heading: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
nodes.start_phrase:
The principal tasks of Group ESG & Sustainability Management, which reports directly to the CEO, include the planning, 
implementation and continued development of RBI’s approach to ESG activities in the function as an internal ESG advisor.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s ESG governance uses a combined top‑down and bottom‑up approach to engage all relevant functions and stakeholders, with ESG officers and ambassadors appointed across subsidiaries to ensure a standardized, coordinated Group-wide framework.
- Group ESG & Sustainability Management, reporting directly to the CEO, acts as the internal ESG advisor and center of expertise, coordinating with specialist departments and subsidiary banks to plan, implement and continually develop ESG activities, set environmental and social targets, and define improvement measures aligned with international standards.
- Together with Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, Group ESG & Sustainability Management oversees proper annual disclosure of non-financial data in the consolidated non-financial statement, manages new and extended reporting requirements, fulfills UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, and engages with ESG rating agencies while serving as a hub for internal and external stakeholders.
- The CFO area leads sustainability and management reporting for sustainable finance, ensuring control, monitoring, data collection, budgeting and reporting; sets policies and frameworks; integrates ESG metrics into the budgeting process; collaborates to ensure data integrity; and, with Sustainable Finance, defines targets for Corporate and Retail businesses. It co-leads the consolidated non-financial statement with Group ESG & Sustainability Management, integrating financial and ESG information for comprehensive, compliant disclosure.
- Group Internal Audit, operating independently on a risk-based basis and steering local audit functions, supports governance bodies, adheres to Global Internal Audit Standards, and undergoes ongoing quality monitoring plus external assessments at least every five years. ESG topics are embedded across audit planning and execution, addressed via dedicated audits or as components within broader audits, with several ESG-specific audits conducted in 2024.

nodes.title: CFO area (Chief Financial Officer)
nodes.heading: CFO area (Chief Financial Officer)
nodes.start_phrase:
The CFO area plays a pivotal role in sustainability and management reporting for sustainable financing, and ensures effective 
control, tracking, monitoring, data collection, budgeting and reporting.
nodes.summary:
- Describes RBI’s ESG governance structure that combines top-down and bottom-up engagement, with ESG officers and ambassadors appointed across subsidiaries to ensure a standardized, coordinated approach.
- Outlines the mandate of Group ESG & Sustainability Management, reporting to the CEO: planning and developing the ESG strategy, advising internally, acting as a central point of contact and expertise, coordinating with specialist departments and CEE/Austrian subsidiaries, and supporting target-setting and improvement measures aligned with international standards.
- Details responsibilities for non-financial reporting: Group ESG & Sustainability Management, together with Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, manages annual disclosure of non-financial data in the consolidated non-financial statement, fulfills UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, and engages with ESG rating agencies.
- Defines the CFO area’s role in sustainability and management reporting for sustainable finance: governance of data collection, control, tracking, monitoring, budgeting, and reporting; setting policies and frameworks; integrating sustainability metrics into budgeting; collaborating to set targets for Corporate and Retail; and co-leading accurate, compliant consolidated non-financial reporting that integrates financial and ESG factors.
- Explains Group Internal Audit’s independent, risk-based oversight: supports governing bodies, maintains independence from business decisions, adheres to group-wide auditing standards and the Global Internal Audit Standards, and ensures quality via continuous monitoring, self-assessments, and external assessments at least every five years.
- Highlights integration of ESG into audit activities across relevant areas, informing annual/quarterly plans and individual audits, with specific ESG topics included in multiple audits in 2024.

nodes.title: Group Internal Audit
nodes.heading: Group Internal Audit
nodes.start_phrase: Group Internal Audit performs its duties throughout the year in accordance with auditing standards that are valid group-wide.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s ESG governance uses both top‑down and bottom‑up engagement to involve all relevant functions and stakeholders, with ESG officers and ambassadors appointed across subsidiaries to ensure a standardized, coordinated approach.
- Group ESG & Sustainability Management, reporting to the CEO, plans, implements, and advances RBI’s ESG strategy as an internal advisor; it coordinates with specialist departments and subsidiary sustainability officers, acts as a central ESG contact and expertise hub, supports setting environmental and social targets, and aligns measures with international standards.
- This group, together with Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, manages annual non‑financial disclosures in the consolidated non‑financial statement, fulfills UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, engages internal and external stakeholders, and works with ESG rating agencies.
- The CFO area leads sustainability and management reporting for sustainable financing, establishing policies, controls, monitoring, data collection, and budgeting to ensure green and social asset reporting aligns with RBI objectives; it integrates ESG metrics into budgeting, collaborates across departments to ensure data integrity, and co‑defines targets for Corporate and Retail with Sustainable Finance.
- The CFO area co‑leads the consolidated non‑financial statement with Group ESG & Sustainability Management, ensuring accurate collection, analysis, and integration of financial and ESG data for comprehensive, compliant reporting.

nodes.title: Sustainability Bond Committee (SBC)

nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Group Regulatory Affairs

nodes.title: Group Compliance
nodes.heading: Group Compliance
nodes.start_phrase:
Group Compliance is responsible for RBI’s compliance framework in line with the three lines of defense model for controlling 
risk management.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines RBI’s Group Compliance function, structured around the three lines of defense, as the owner of the compliance framework and a key stakeholder in climate- and sustainability-related regulation.
- Group Compliance monitors statutory and regulatory requirements, proposes policy updates, gives expert input on sector policies, recommends follow-up measures, and reviews sustainable financing products.
- It mitigates greenwashing and human rights risks across the value chain through guidance and controls, and covers core compliance areas including financial sanctions, anti-money laundering, fraud and bribery prevention, and conflicts of interest.
- Governance presence includes representation on the Sustainability, Sustainability Bond, Sustainable Deposit, and Remuneration Committees; in 2023, ESG compliance competencies were centralized in Capital Markets Compliance to ensure consistent coverage of sustainability, sensitive business, and human rights topics.
- Internal Controls, within Group Compliance, operates the Internal Control System (ICS) using a processes/risks/controls approach aligned with the three lines of defense and the COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework.
- The ICS involves ongoing risk identification, control design and documentation, prioritization, and independent testing; roles are defined for 1st line (processes/controls), 2nd line (challenge/validation), and 3rd line (Internal Audit assurance).
- ICS activities are reported to the Operational Risks Management and Controls Committee, the Management Board, and the Audit Committee.
- Internal Controls governs internal control over financial and sustainability reporting, with priorities for sustainability reporting including clear internal communication, process mapping and documentation, and key controls to ensure completeness and timeliness.
- Credit Portfolio Management, within Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management (reporting to the CRO), sets risk appetite and portfolio limits and leads ESG risk steering and implementation across the risk organization.
- Financials Risk Management and Financials Rating & Analysis ensure ESG integration for financial institution counterparties; other ESG topics (e.g., steering measure operationalization, disclosure compliance) are managed within the respective risk areas.

nodes.title: Facility Management

nodes.summary:
- Facility Management: Reports to the COO and ensures smooth head office operations at RBI, overseeing energy use, waste and water management, selected office material procurement (e.g., paper), postal services, and logistics. Implements local sustainability measures (e.g., smart temperature control, energy-efficient lighting) and collects operational data to calculate, track, and reduce emissions.

- Environmental Committee: Established in 1994 by the Management Board as the advisory and decision-making body for environmental management at head office. Chaired by the Environmental Officer with permanent members from Group ESG & Sustainability, Group Procurement, Group IT, and the Staff Council; other experts join as needed. Meets at least twice a year to develop decision principles for ecological strategies, plan initiatives, and conduct assessments and weak-point analyses.

- Policy framework and governance: Policies serve as core governance tools, comprising directives (regulatory implementation), general instructions (broad employee impact), and specific instructions with supporting documents (internal governance). The Management Board approves directives and general instructions; senior management approves specific instructions and supporting documents. Policies are binding with defined scopes, apply to Group units (credit institutions and units with >10 employees, operative, fully consolidated per CRR), and must be locally implemented. An exception process exists for local legal or business-model constraints, requiring local Board approval and final authorization by the relevant authority/Group Policy Owner. The RBI policy database is the single source for internal policies, accessible to affected employees, with regular notifications on updates; all policies must be updated as required by law or at least every two years.

nodes.title: Environmental Committee
nodes.heading: Environmental Committee
nodes.start_phrase:
In accordance with their responsibility for environmental measures, the Management Board members at RBI AG appointed an 
Environmental Officer and an Environmental Committee in 1994.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines RBI’s operational sustainability governance. Facility Management, reporting to the COO, oversees head office operations including energy, water, waste, office material procurement (e.g., paper), postal services, and logistics, and implements local sustainability measures such as smart temperature controls and energy‑saving lighting. It collects operational data to calculate, track, and reduce emissions. The Environmental Committee, established in 1994, serves as the advisory and decision-making body for environmental and sustainability matters at head office, convening at least twice a year; it is led by the Environmental Officer with permanent members from Group ESG & Sustainability Management, Group Procurement, Group IT, and the Staff Council, and conducts strategy development, planning, status assessments, and weak-point analyses. The policy framework defines three policy types—regulatory directives, general instructions, and specific instructions with supporting documents—with approval by the Management Board (directives/general) or senior management (specific/supporting). Policies are binding, scoped by policy owners, and must be implemented by affected RBI Group units (credit institutions and fully consolidated operative units with more than ten employees), with a formal exception process for local legal conflicts or business model constraints requiring local Board and Group approvals. A centralized policy database serves as the authoritative source; employees are notified of updates, and policies are reviewed at least biennially or as required by law.

nodes.title: Policy frameworks as governance instruments
nodes.heading: Policy frameworks as governance instruments
nodes.start_phrase: Policies are a cornerstone of governance and managing impacts, risks and opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- Facility Management
  - Reports to the COO and ensures smooth head-office operations.
  - Manages energy, water, waste, select office material procurement (e.g., paper), postal services, and logistics.
  - Implements local sustainability initiatives (e.g., smart temperature control, energy‑saving lighting).
  - Collects head-office operational data to calculate and track emissions and enable swift reduction measures.

- Environmental Committee
  - Established by the Management Board in 1994; serves as advisory and decision-making body for operational environmental management and sustainability at head office.
  - Permanent members: Environmental Officer, Group ESG & Sustainability Management, Group Procurement, Group IT, and Staff Council; additional experts join as needed.
  - Meets at least twice a year; tasks include developing decision principles for ecological strategies and initiatives, and conducting status assessments and weak-point analyses.

- Policy frameworks as governance instruments
  - Policy types: regulatory directives, general instructions, and specific governance instructions with supporting documents.
  - Approvals: Management Board approves directives and general instructions; senior management approves specific instructions and supporting documents.
  - Policies are binding; scope defined by policy owners and approved authorities.
  - Applies to all Group units in scope (credit institutions and units with >10 employees, operative, fully consolidated per CRR).
  - Mandatory local implementation; formal exception process for conflicts (e.g., local law, business model constraints) requiring local Board and Group-level approvals.
  - Central policy database as the official source; employees receive updates; policies reviewed per law or at least biennially.

- Information to and oversight by governing bodies (GOV-2)
  - Management Board, Supervisory Board, and committees receive regular updates on material impacts, risks, and opportunities from senior management (incl. CRO and sustainability officers).
  - Oversight focuses on aligning strategy and risk management with sustainability goals, assessing trade-offs in major decisions.

- 2024 Management Board focus areas (per Sustainability Committee recommendations)
  - ESG business transformation, acceleration of ESG data collection, embedding ESG in business practice, ESG communication and stakeholder engagement, and regulatory compliance.

- Key topics discussed in 2024
  - Overall sustainability management
    - Non-financial KPIs integrated into Board members’ performance agreements.
    - CSRD implementation updates (impacts, risks, opportunities, internal controls and processes).
    - ESG ratings and contentious issues.
  - Environmental
    - Financed emissions target; climate and environmental business strategy and transition plan; client engagement strategy.
    - Sector policies (steel; real estate & construction); ESG Business Rulebook and greenwashing prevention.
    - ESG risk management: internal climate stress test, ECB Fit‑for‑55 exercise, EBA ESG Pillar 3 ITS disclosures, financed emissions calculation, ESG data management, EU Taxonomy, and other supervisory/regulatory matters.
  - Social
    - 2024 employee engagement survey results; updates to diversity, human rights, and defense policies.
    - Own workforce topics: executive and leadership development, social allowances, performance and reward, AI operating model and Pioneers Project, learning and development budget priorities, impacts of the Russia/Ukraine war on employees.
    - Cybersecurity strategy, roadmap, and status; tax compliance and transparency; data privacy (breaches, Data Subject Rights, privacy impact assessments).
  - Governance
    - Code of Conduct update; ESG governance (Sustainability Committee).
    - Regular compliance updates (AML, sanctions, governance and controls, financial crime, capital market and regulatory compliance).
    - Bylaws for Sustainable Deposit Committee, Sustainability Bond Committee, and Sustainability Committee.

nodes.title: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.heading: GOV-2: Information provided to and sustainability matters add ressed by administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.start_phrase:
The Management Board, the Supervisory Board and relevant committees are informed on a regular basis about material 
impacts, risks, and opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- Governance oversight of sustainability (GOV-2): Management and Supervisory Boards receive regular, structured updates from senior management (CRO and sustainability officers) on material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs). This informs oversight of strategy, major transactions, and risk management, including trade-off assessments that balance short-term outcomes with long-term sustainability goals.

- 2024 ESG priorities: ESG transformation of the business, acceleration of ESG data collection, deeper integration of ESG into business practice, strengthened ESG communication and stakeholder engagement, and ESG regulatory compliance.

- Sustainability management topics: Introduction of non-financial KPIs as mandatory elements of Management Board members’ performance agreements; regular progress on CSRD implementation with focus on IROs, internal controls, and processes; updates on ESG ratings and contentious issues.

- Environmental focus: Financed emissions target setting and methodology; climate and environmental business strategy and transition plan; client engagement strategy; sector policies (steel; real estate & construction); ESG Business Rulebook with greenwashing prevention; ESG risk management including internal climate stress test results, ECB Fit-for-55 exercise, EBA ESG Pillar 3 disclosures, EU Taxonomy developments, and ESG data management.

- Social focus: 2024 employee engagement survey results; updates on diversity, human rights, and defense policies; workforce initiatives (executive and leadership development, social allowances, performance and reward, AI operating model and Pioneers Project, strategic L&D budget), support related to the Russia/Ukraine war; cyber security strategy/roadmap and status; tax compliance and transparency; data privacy (breaches, Data Subject Rights, privacy impact assessments).

- Governance focus: Code of Conduct update; ESG governance (Sustainability Committee); ongoing compliance updates (anti-money laundering, sanctions, compliance governance and controls, financial crime, capital market and regulatory compliance); bylaws for Sustainable Deposit, Sustainability Bond, and Sustainability Committees.

- Material topics reported to the Supervisory Board: Climate change, regulatory compliance, sustainable finance (including CSRD implementation), ESG risks, and diversity.

- Incentives and remuneration (GOV-3): Remuneration framework supports long-term strategy, transparency, prudent risk-taking, and conflict-of-interest safeguards. Fixed pay is non-performance-based. Variable pay is determined by Return-on-Equity and Cost-Income-Ratio targets at RBI AG and subsidiaries, subject to regulatory/performance criteria; at least 40% deferred over up to five years; 50% delivered as phantom shares with one-year retention. Malus/clawback enables ex-post risk adjustment. Non-financial KPIs for Management Board members indicate linkage to sustainability objectives within performance management.

nodes.title: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes
nodes.heading: GOV-3 : Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes
nodes.start_phrase: Remuneration is based on four underlying principles:
nodes.summary:
- Oversight of ESG topics: In 2024, the Management Board briefed the Supervisory Board on key sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, including climate strategy and risk mitigation, ESG regulatory compliance (e.g., CSRD), sustainable finance initiatives, ESG risk monitoring, and workplace diversity.
- Integration of sustainability into remuneration (GOV-3): Remuneration principles align pay with long-term strategy, transparent performance measurement, sound risk management, and conflict-of-interest safeguards. Fixed pay is non-performance-based; variable pay depends on step-in criteria and KPIs (Return on Equity and Cost-Income Ratio), with deferrals (≥40% for larger bonuses) over up to five years and 50% delivered via phantom shares with a one-year retention. Malus/clawback mechanisms enable ex-post risk adjustments.
- 2024 ESG Board objectives and performance: 
  - All Board Members: Gender diversity targets (RBI 35% in 2024; RBI AG 30% by 2026) and fostering a high-performing, attractive workplace culture.
  - CEO: Grow new ESG business volumes.
  - CRO: Implement ESG regulatory requirements, CO2 target setting at portfolio/industry level, embed ESG in approvals, develop GAR and Banking Book Taxonomy KPIs/processes, ensure timely compliance, and strengthen ESG risk governance and learning.
  - COO/CIO: Advance in-house ecology (IT baseline per ESG cockpit, HO Vienna green energy efficiency) and support digital talent development (School 42).
  - Retail Banking: Decarbonize retail loans, enhance emissions/energy-efficiency data collection, achieve 10% new sales in green/social retail loans and ESG investments, prevent greenwashing via training, and expand financial literacy.
  - Corporate & Investment Banking: Deliver €7bn in sustainable financing, reach 47% ESG funds AUM group-wide, 35% ESG certificates, complete ESG transition policy, set targets for 50% of financed emissions, and provide top-tier ESG advisory.
  - 2024 evaluation emphasized responsible customers/business volume, climate/environmental transformation, sustainable financing, ESG regulatory and risk management, diversity, in-house ecology, and cybersecurity; climate factors focused on implementing CO2 targets, approval process integration, and Green Deal assessment.
- 2025 ESG Board objectives:
  - All Board Members: Country-specific People & Culture targets for an attractive, high-performing organization.
  - CEO: Oversee group-wide ESG asset outcomes and implement 2030 CO2 targets aligned with RBI’s transition plan.
  - CFO: Establish advanced ESG reporting, steer ESG business generation, and embed ESG-eligible bond issuance in funding.
  - CRO: Set and commit to a 2026–2030 path to meet 2030 CO2 targets and bolster ESG data collection.
  - COO/CIO: Support a 1.5°C-aligned transition plan for own operations.
  - Corporate & Investment Banking: Ensure up to 20% ESG-conform year-end corporate assets per the ESG Rulebook; support sustainable funding (e.g., MREL Green, Supranationals); implement local CO2 target plans and engagement strategies focused on high emitters; maintain 47% ESG funds AUM.
  - Retail Banking: Achieve 10% of new retail loans as green/social and €580m in ESG investments; support sustainable funding and financed-emissions target setting.
- Bonus determination framework: Board member bonuses require meeting minimum step-in criteria and are calculated by KPI achievement; performance mix includes at least 40% financial and up to 60% non-financial (strategic execution, efficiency, innovation, customer satisfaction, risk/governance/compliance, employee engagement, leadership, and environmental/social responsibility).
- Supervisory Board remuneration: No variable pay; members receive fixed annual compensation approved by the General Assembly.

nodes.title: Approval process and governance
nodes.heading: Approval process and governance
nodes.start_phrase:
The remuneration policy for the Management Board and the Supervisory Board is drawn up by the Supervisory Board, and the 
Supervisory Board’s Remuneration Committee, established within RBI AG pursuant to § 39c of the Austrian Banking Act, submits 
its recommended decision to the Supervisory Board.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Governance framework for remuneration at RBI AG, focusing on the Management Board and alignment with Austrian Banking Act requirements.
- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Supervisory Board drafts the remuneration policy for the Management and Supervisory Boards; the Remuneration Committee (per §39c Austrian Banking Act) prepares recommendations and resolutions for the Supervisory Board.
  - Annual General Meeting votes (advisory) on the remuneration policy at legal intervals and on the annual Remuneration Report; votes are recommendatory.
  - Personnel Committee decides on Management Board employment contracts and remuneration terms; sets and adjusts targets, determines target achievement, and approves bonus allocations.
  - Remuneration Committee and/or Personnel Committee decide on malus and clawback events and consequences.
- Approval/decision matrix highlights:
  - Remuneration policy and Remuneration Report: Remuneration Committee recommends; Supervisory Board authorizes; AGM holds advisory vote.
  - General remuneration principles (identified staff, incl. Management Board) and performance management rules: authorized by the Remuneration Committee.
  - Individual Management Board targets, appraisals, and bonus amounts: authorized by the Remuneration Committee.
  - Management Board contracts: decided by the Personnel Committee.
  - Periodic review of the remuneration policy: decided by the Supervisory Board and reviewed with AGM advisory input.
- Remuneration Report requirements:
  - Clear, comprehensive disclosure of all remuneration awarded or owed to current/former Management Board members, including targets, target achievement, and linkage to business strategy and long-term growth.
  - Public disclosure; subsequent reports must explain how prior AGM voting feedback was considered.
- Compliance and risk oversight:
  - Remuneration Committee issues detailed guidelines to implement §39b Austrian Banking Act (BWG) for identified staff and Management Board performance management.
  - Ongoing monitoring of remuneration policy, practices, and incentives regarding risk management, capital adequacy, and liquidity, considering long-term interests of shareholders, investors, employees, and financial stability.
- Controls and assurance:
  - Internal control functions are involved in the design, implementation, and review of remuneration policy.
  - At least annual independent internal review of policy implementation; use of independent external consultants as needed.

nodes.title: Statement on due diligence
nodes.heading: GOV-4 : Statement on due diligence
nodes.start_phrase: The financial services sector itself has for years been confronted with many challenges and risks.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines RBI’s due diligence approach within its consolidated non-financial statement, mapping core due diligence elements to ESRS disclosures: embedding in governance/strategy/business model; stakeholder engagement; identification and assessment of adverse impacts; actions to address them; and tracking, targets, and communication (including GOV-5 on internal controls over sustainability reporting).
- It specifies where related policies and processes are disclosed, covering governance oversight (GOV-2, GOV-3), materiality and strategy integration (SBM-3, IRO-1), stakeholder engagement across workers, consumers, suppliers, and climate policies (SBM-2, E1-2, S1-1/2, S4-1/2, G1-1/2), and target-setting (E1-4, S1-5).
- The preparation of the consolidated non-financial statement involves cross-functional collaboration (Group ESG & Sustainability, Accounting & Financial Methodologies, Risk Controlling, People & Culture, Facility Management), data collection within divisions, and use of the Workiva platform to ensure simultaneous editing, automation, transparency, and robust change tracking; final approval follows division head sign-off and submission to the Management Board and Supervisory Board.
- RBI prioritizes a balanced, compliant report with an internal control and risk management system (ICS) covering non-financial reporting to prevent misstatements; two key reporting risks are identified—omission of material topics and inaccurate data—mitigated by a pre-report materiality assessment and dual controls in contributing divisions.
- ESG risk management is integrated across the enterprise risk organization to support RBI’s long-term, responsible banking strategy and meet ECB/EBA expectations, with progress tracked via internal ESG KPIs.
- The ESG risk framework applies across four pillars:
  - Identification and definition: climate and environmental risks (climate change, circularity, biodiversity), social risks, governance risks.
  - Measurement and analytics: customer/portfolio ESG metrics, ESG scores, Green Asset Ratio, financed GHG emissions, climate stress testing.
  - Steering: sectoral strategies and special policies, prevention of liability, reputational, and greenwashing risks in design.
  - Risk processes and governance: enhanced credit processes and an ESG Risk Policy Statement; ESG topics are addressed through the CRO line organization for day-to-day integration.
- The ESG risk framework is reviewed annually, updated to reflect trends and stakeholder expectations, and approved by the Management Board.

nodes.title: Risk framework
nodes.heading: Risk framework
nodes.start_phrase: Risk management is essential for implementing the ESG strategy and the associated risk control measures.
nodes.summary:
- Identifies two key risks in the consolidated non-financial statement: missing material topics and inaccurate data.
- Describes mitigations: a pre-report materiality assessment to ensure topic completeness and dual control checks within divisions to ensure data accuracy.
- Presents RBI’s ESG risk framework as integral to the overall risk organization and ESG strategy execution.
- Notes the initial focus on climate and environmental risks (transition and physical) assessed at counterparty level and via materiality assessment and internal/external climate stress tests, with growing emphasis on social and governance risks.
- Details integration of ESG risks into the four pillars of risk management:
  - Identification and definition of ESG risks (climate change, circularity, biodiversity; social and governance risks).
  - Measurement methodologies and analytics (ESG scores, Green Asset Ratio, financed GHG emissions, climate stress testing).
  - Steering approaches reflecting risks and opportunities (sectoral strategies, special policies, prevention of liability, reputational, and greenwashing risks in design).
  - Risk processes and governance (credit process enhancements, ESG Risk Policy Statement).
- Explains that ESG topics are managed through the CRO line organization to embed them in daily business, aligning with ECB and EBA guidance and RBI’s business model.
- States progress tracking via internal ESG KPIs and regular monitoring.
- Confirms the ESG risk framework is reviewed and updated annually based on trends and stakeholder expectations, and approved by the Management Board.

nodes.title: Identification of ESG risks
nodes.heading: Identification of ESG risks
nodes.start_phrase: Proper identification, definition and understanding of ESG risks are crucial.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on properly identifying, defining, and understanding ESG risks, with initial focus on climate and environmental risks; social and governance risks are gaining prominence amid new regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- Methodological approach combines qualitative, expert-driven work with quantitative tools: impact and materiality assessments, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests.
- Organization-wide knowledge transfer through mandatory ESG risk training for risk staff and regular training/exchange sessions across RBI and its subsidiaries.
- Environmental risks defined via an outside-in lens: financial impacts from counterparties exposed to climate change and environmental degradation (air/water pollution, water scarcity, land contamination, biodiversity loss, deforestation), leading to physical and transition risks and potentially higher capital needs, costs, revenue losses, and deterioration in credit quality; transmission to traditional risk types (market, liquidity, credit, operational) noted.
- Social risks framed as financial impacts from misuse of human capital (working conditions, health and safety, diversity, training, inclusiveness, equality, community programs); ESG scoring incorporates country-specific social standards, affecting customer scores.
- Governance risks tied to counterparties’ governance practices and integration of ESG in policies (executive pay, board structure/diversity, shareholder rights, anti-bribery/corruption, compliance, ethical standards including data ethics, fair tax strategy).
- Measurement methodologies and analytics focus on creating, collecting, and sourcing ESG data, with references to estimation and outcome uncertainty.
- Steering and strategy: commitments and policies addressing thermal coal, nuclear power, arms and war material, and gambling; development of sector-specific policies for high CO2 emitters and sectors with negative impacts on circularity and biodiversity; references to related policy and climate stress testing disclosures.

nodes.title: Measurement methodologies & analytics
nodes.heading: Measurement methodologies & analytics
nodes.start_phrase: This chapter focuses on data creation, collection and data sourcing.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines RBI’s approach to identifying, defining, and understanding ESG risks, with an initial emphasis on climate-related and environmental risks, while increasingly integrating social and governance aspects in line with evolving regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- RBI complements qualitative, expert-driven assessments with quantitative tools such as impact and materiality analyses, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests; ESG risk training is mandatory across the risk function and shared group-wide.
- Financed emissions are used to pinpoint carbon-intensive industries in the non-retail portfolio, with detailed results referenced in a dedicated emissions chapter.
- Environmental risks are framed from an outside-in perspective as financial risks arising from counterparties’ exposure to climate change and environmental degradation (e.g., pollution, water scarcity, biodiversity loss), as well as compliance pressures; these can translate into physical and transition risks affecting capital, costs, revenues, and credit quality, with transmission to market, liquidity, credit, and operational risks.
- Social risks relate to the financial impacts of mismanaging human capital (e.g., labor conditions, health and safety, diversity, inclusion), with country-specific social standards influencing customer ESG scores.
- Governance risks cover counterparties’ governance practices (e.g., executive pay, board structure, shareholder rights, anti-corruption, compliance, data ethics, fair tax), including how ESG is embedded in policies and procedures.
- Measurement and analytics emphasize data creation, collection, and sourcing, with further detail provided in a chapter on estimation sources and uncertainty.
- Steering actions include commitments and policies for sensitive sectors (thermal coal, nuclear power, arms and war material, gambling) and evolving sector-specific policies targeting high CO2 emitters and activities with adverse circularity/biodiversity impacts; references are provided to chapters on climate policies and stress test results.

nodes.title: Steering approaches, reflecting risk and opportunities
nodes.heading: Steering approaches, reflecting risk and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase:
Due to its market position RBI takes responsibility to redefine and reshape its business in line with the latest market and 
regulatory requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: RBI’s ESG risk framework prioritizes climate-related and environmental risks while increasingly integrating social and governance risks in line with evolving regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- Risk identification and assessment: Starts with a qualitative, expert-driven approach, now complemented by quantitative tools such as impact and materiality assessments, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests; transmission channels to traditional risk types are defined and elaborated separately.
- Organizational enablement: ESG risk knowledge is cascaded across RBI and its subsidiaries via training and exchange sessions; ESG risk training is mandatory for risk staff.
- Financed emissions: Used to identify carbon-intensive sectors in the non-retail portfolio; detailed metrics are referenced in chapter E1-6 (Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions).
- Environmental (E) risks: Defined via an outside-in lens as financial risks from counterparties exposed to climate change and environmental degradation (e.g., pollution, water scarcity, biodiversity loss, deforestation), including physical and transition risk drivers that can affect capital needs, costs, revenues, and credit standing; links to market, liquidity, credit, and operational risk are detailed elsewhere.
- Social (S) risks: Cover financial impacts of misuse of human capital (e.g., labor conditions, health and safety, diversity, training, inclusion); ESG scoring incorporates country-level social standards, so identical corporates may differ in scores by jurisdiction.
- Governance (G) risks: Concern counterparties’ governance quality and integration of ESG into policies (e.g., executive pay, board diversity, shareholder rights, anti-bribery, compliance, ethics, data ethics, tax fairness).
- Measurement methodologies and analytics: Emphasis on data creation, collection, and sourcing; further detail in “Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty.”
- Steering and sector policies: RBI commits to aligning business with regulatory/market expectations, with specific commitments in thermal coal, nuclear power, arms/war material, and gambling; evolving sector-specific policies target high-CO2 and high negative impacts on circularity and biodiversity.
- Disclosures and references: Policies on climate mitigation/adaptation in chapter E1-2; climate stress testing results in the Climate stress testing chapter.

nodes.title: Risk processes and governance
nodes.heading: Risk processes and governance
nodes.start_phrase: The Management Board is the most senior decision-making body for ESG-related strategies, policies and commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure: ESG strategies, policies and commitments are led by the Management Board, with environmental risk tools and reports pre-approved by the Group Risk Committee and supported by a cross-functional Sustainability Committee.
- ESG risk integration: ESG risks are treated as cross-dimensional drivers embedded across market, operational, liquidity and credit risk, with measurement over short-, medium- and long-term horizons. Materiality assessments inform implementation and ongoing enhancement of the ICAAP.
- Risk appetite and ICAAP: Group risk tolerance is set below 100% of overall risk capacity. Transition and physical (flood) climate risks, informed by climate stress tests, are recognized as deductions from Pillar 2 internal capital (from Q1 2022). Environmental risk drivers have been included in group risk assessment since 2021, and are budgeted within the short-term (up to three years) risk appetite.
- Methodologies and standards: Scenario analysis and materiality assessments use NGFS frameworks and scenarios aligned with EU climate objectives; physical risk impacts are assessed under NGFS transition scenarios. Financed emissions reduction targets align with EU 2030 goals. Additional standards are set out in the RBI Group ESG Rulebook.
- Tools and policies (as of end-2024): ESG score; Green Asset Ratio (GAR); financed GHG emissions; sector business policies (nuclear energy, steel, oil & gas, real estate and construction, thermal coal); RBI Group ESG Rulebook; ESG risk framework; climate stress test methodology and results; ICAAP treatment of transition and physical risks.
- Reporting: ESG risk reporting is embedded in the risk controlling framework and presented regularly to the Group Risk Committee. Quarterly reports include financed emissions, physical risk/vulnerability, energy efficiency distribution, exposure to top polluters, ESG rating distribution, and GAR; climate stress tests are reported annually.
- Sustainability strategy (SBM-1): RBI defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity for long-term economic success while considering social and environmental aspects, embedding it in leadership and management. Through an ESG & Sustainability Policy, RBI focuses on areas with significant impacts on economy, environment and people (including human rights), aiming to enhance positive impacts, reduce negatives, and measure both.
- Strategic drivers and focus: Sustainability is integrated into business strategy, driven by regulation, supervisory expectations, and stakeholder demands (investors, customers, employees). The group-wide strategy “RBI creates sustainable value” centers on three action areas—responsible banker, fair partner, engaged citizen—covering economy, environment and society, and is operationalized via nine core action areas that are continuously refined with stakeholder input.

nodes.title: Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.heading: SBM-1 : Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.start_phrase: Key elements of strategy that relate to sustainability matters.
nodes.summary: The document outlines Raiffeisen Bank International’s sustainability strategy and how it is embedded in its overall business model and value chain. It defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity that achieves long-term economic success while considering key social and environmental aspects, positioning it as a core leadership and management responsibility. RBI’s ESG & Sustainability Policy sets the strategic approach to integrate sustainability into business activities, focusing on areas with significant impacts on the economy, environment, and people, including human rights. The bank commits to enhancing positive impacts, reducing negative ones, and developing measurement and verification methods to support long-term value creation and societal development. External drivers include evolving regulation, supervisory expectations, and growing demands from investors, customers, and employees for sustainable products, services, and tangible outcomes. The group-wide strategy, “RBI creates sustainable value,” is structured around three strategic action areas—responsible banker, fair partner, and engaged citizen—aligned with the pillars of economy, environment, and society. It identifies nine core action areas to guide group-wide sustainability management, with priorities continuously refined based on stakeholder perspectives.

nodes.title: RBI’s understanding of sustainability
nodes.heading: RBI’s u nderstanding of sustainability
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability is a fundamental principle for RBI and a measure of corporate success.
nodes.summary:
- RBI positions sustainability as a core corporate principle and a measure of success, combining financial performance with social responsibility built over 130+ years.
- Defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity that delivers long-term economic results while considering key social and environmental aspects, linked to corporate culture.
- Embeds sustainability into leadership, management structures, processes, and daily business activities; it is an explicit part of the overall business strategy and value chain.
- Establishes an ESG & Sustainability Policy to guide strategic integration of sustainability across operations.
- Focuses on three strategic responsibility areas—responsible banker, fair partner, engaged citizen—each aligned to the pillars of economy, environment, and society.
- Aims to prioritize areas with significant impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights), enhance positive impacts, reduce negative ones, and develop metrics to measure and verify outcomes.
- Seeks to create long-term corporate value while contributing to sustainable societal development.
- Identifies key drivers for a concrete sustainability strategy: evolving regulations, supervisory expectations, and growing demands from investors, customers (for sustainable products/services), and employees (for real impact and results).
- Introduces a group-wide strategy, “RBI creates sustainable value,” comprising the three action areas and nine core action areas for sustainability management, with priorities updated continuously based on stakeholder perspectives.

nodes.title: RBI’s sustainability strategy
nodes.heading: RBI’s sustainability strategy
nodes.start_phrase: In order to improve the effectiveness and scope of sustainability management across RBI as a whole, RBI has published the group-wide sustainability strategy : RBI creates sustainable value.
nodes.summary:
- Presents SBM-1: Strategy, business model and value chain, focusing on sustainability as a core principle of RBI and a measure of corporate success.
- Defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity aimed at long-term economic outcomes while considering key social and environmental aspects, embedded in corporate culture, leadership, and management processes.
- Outlines three strategic sustainability areas—responsible banker, fair partner, engaged citizen—closely linked to business activities to drive sustainable development within RBI and society.
- Describes an ESG & Sustainability Policy that formalizes integrating sustainability into business activities.
- Emphasizes focusing on material impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights), with commitments to enhance positive impacts, reduce negatives, and establish measurement and verification.
- Positions sustainability as part of RBI’s business strategy, driven by regulation, supervisory expectations, and stakeholder demands (investors, customers, consumers, and employees).
- Introduces the group-wide strategy “RBI creates sustainable value,” structured around the three action areas and nine core action areas, with priorities refined continuously based on stakeholder perspectives.

nodes.title: Core action areas of RBI’s sustainability strategy
nodes.heading: Core action areas of RBI’s sustainability str ategy
nodes.start_phrase: The most effective leverage for a bank is in its core business, namely in granting loans and investing funds.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines RBI’s sustainability matrix across Economy, Society, and Environment, structured around three roles:
