  - Responsible banker: value creation, social and ecological product responsibility (consumer protection, data protection, transparent information; compliance with environmental laws and conventions; integrating environmental impacts in finance and products).
  - Fair partner: fair business and operating practices, stakeholder inclusion, and in-house ecology (anti-corruption, transparent reporting, attractive employer; systematic stakeholder engagement; reducing own environmental footprint and meeting group climate targets).
  - Engaged citizen: sustainable entrepreneurship, active civil society, environmentally friendly society (supporting sustainable finance frameworks and social initiatives; financial literacy and volunteering; climate action, biodiversity, and ecosystem protection).
- Emphasizes core-business leverage in lending and investing to build long-term resilience, avoid social and environmental risks, and advance higher standards; grounded in trust and reliability.
- Confirms RBI’s commitment to sustainable development in Austria and CEE, making ESG central to strategy with measurable positive impacts, science-based CO2 targets, alignment with EU ESG regulations, and adherence to UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Describes governance and execution: assessing positive/negative ESG impacts, setting improvement goals, adapting products/services, fostering a sustainability-oriented culture, proactive stakeholder engagement, and transparent reporting.
- Details the climate and environmental business strategy:
  - 2024 update with Management Board–approved emissions targets.
  - Gradual integration of qualitative/quantitative criteria into business processes to manage the portfolio sustainably.
  - Reducing exposure to companies that fail climate/environmental criteria or lack credible transition pathways.
  - Supporting customers’ climate and ecological transition through transition pathways, ESG expertise, and sustainable finance solutions to increase climate-friendly transactions.
  - Regular reviews reflecting scientific advances, portfolio ESG insights, and clients’ transformation progress; sector-specific tailoring where needed.
- Introduces three strategic pillars aligned with regulatory requirements and UNEP FI commitments; the first pillar focuses on Paris Agreement alignment by:
  - Embedding climate and environmental factors in lending decisions, risk and operational control, and resource allocation.
  - Expanding the use of assets for sustainable financing products.

nodes.title: RBI’s climate and environmental business strategy
nodes.heading: RBI’s climate and environmental business strategy
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the climate and environmental business strategy was further developed by setting emissions targets which were approved by the Management Board.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines RBI’s sustainability matrix across economy, society and environment, detailing responsibilities in core banking (value creation), social and ecological product responsibility, fair business practices, stakeholder engagement, in‑house ecology, sustainable entrepreneurship, active civil society and an environmentally friendly society.
- Emphasizes the bank’s greatest leverage through core activities—lending and investing—aimed at long‑term resilience, avoidance of social and environmental risks, and seizing sustainability opportunities, underpinned by trust and reliability.
- Confirms commitment to integrate ESG into strategy and operations in Austria and CEE, pursue measurable positive impacts, set science‑based CO2 targets, follow EU ESG regulations, and align with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Describes a climate and environmental business strategy with 2024 Board‑approved emissions targets, integrating qualitative and quantitative criteria into processes to manage portfolios sustainably and limit exposure to companies lacking credible transition pathways.
- Details continuous review of the strategy based on scientific advances, portfolio ESG insights, and client transformation progress, with sector‑specific adaptation.
- Presents three strategic pillars:
  1) Align portfolios with the Paris Agreement by embedding climate and environmental factors in lending, risk, operations and resource allocation, and growing sustainable financing assets.
  2) Support clients’ transition via expertise and practical, innovative sustainable products and services, prioritizing positive environmental and social impacts in CEE.
  3) Advance sustainable finance through robust ESG expertise and governance, including ESG policies, an ESG risk framework and greenwashing prevention processes.
- Highlights corporate and institutional client offering: tailored sustainable finance instruments (loans, bonds, promissory notes, guarantees, derivatives), including sustainability‑linked, ESG rating‑linked and use‑of‑proceeds formats, aligned with EU rules and LMA/ICMA standards.
- Stresses collaborative KPI setting for ESG‑linked financings to ensure materiality and ambition; support spans all sectors, from critical (e.g., oil and gas) to renewables.
- Describes roles across transactions (arranger, bookrunner, sustainability structuring advisor, lender) and comprehensive client support on EU Taxonomy alignment, access to subsidies, ESG ratings, second‑party opinions, SBTi/net‑zero topics and portfolio decarbonization strategies.
- Notes stakeholder engagement, transparency, data protection, anti‑corruption, and internal environmental measures to meet group climate targets, alongside initiatives to promote financial literacy and broader societal and environmental stewardship.

nodes.title: Corporate & institutional clients business
nodes.heading: Corporate & institutional clients business
nodes.start_phrase: RBI serves around 134,000 corporate clients across CEE (including medium-sized businesses, large local companies, international corporations and local authorities) as well as local and international institutional clients.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s second pillar centers on helping customers transition to climate- and environment-friendly practices by providing expertise, innovative financial products, and increased impact investments, with a focus on Central and Eastern Europe.
- The third pillar advances sustainable financing through strong ESG expertise and governance, including establishing ESG policies such as an ESG risk framework and anti-greenwashing processes, and building/maintaining internal knowledge.
- Corporate and institutional clients: RBI serves ~134,000 clients across CEE (from mid-sized firms to international corporations and public sector), offering tailored solutions in financing, capital markets advisory, risk hedging, and transaction banking.
- Sustainable finance offering: wide range of instruments (bonds, promissory notes, syndicated/bilateral loans) linked to ESG ratings, sustainability targets, or use-of-proceeds; support in identifying/defining sustainable transactions aligned with EU regulations and LMA/ICMA standards; EU Taxonomy alignment and internal green/social/sustainable definitions.
- KPI setting: collaborative definition of material, ambitious ESG KPIs tied to clients’ sustainability and business strategies, with annual targets aimed at demonstrable improvement.
- Sector coverage: tailored solutions across all sectors, including critical (e.g., oil and gas) and non-critical (e.g., renewables), ensuring clarity on market standards, requirements, and best practices.
- Transaction roles and formats: acts as arranger, bookrunner, sustainability structuring advisor, and lender; provides loans, promissory notes, bonds, guarantees, derivatives; supports sustainability-linked, ESG rating-linked, and use-of-proceeds formats.
- Additional client support: guidance on EU Taxonomy, access to subsidized financing and EU/Austria programs; assistance with ESG ratings and second-party opinions; advisory on net zero and Science Based Targets initiative.
- Capacity building and strategy: delivers ESG education for institutional clients; supports strategic credit portfolio transformation toward carbon neutrality and SDGs; helps develop ESG and sustainable financing strategies, shift internal perspectives, and manage ongoing ESG processes and trends.

nodes.title: Retail business
nodes.heading: Retail business
nodes.start_phrase: RBI provides services to around 18 million retail, private banking and small business customers, offering a broad product range (e.g. account packages, clearing, settlement and payment services, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgage loans and investment products).
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s retail segment serves ~18 million retail, private banking, and small business customers with a broad product suite: account packages, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, and investment products.
- In Austria, retail investment advisory and asset management are provided via Kathrein Privatbank; housing loans via Raiffeisen Bausparkasse; card business at RBI’s head office.
- Responsible banking is embedded in the Group Strategic Roadmap (since 2023), focusing on supporting customers’ green transition through:
  - Tools to understand customer carbon footprints.
  - Expanded sustainability-oriented products with environmental and social impact.
  - Growth targets for green and social lending (green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgages) to private individuals and small businesses.
- Investment products:
  - Advisory for funds, certificates, and green bond issuance.
  - Sustainable investment of customer deposits primarily via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft (Raiffeisen Capital Management), offering securities and real estate funds and investment management.
  - Sales focus on Austria with key markets in Italy, Germany, and CEE; Austrian distribution via Raiffeisen Banking Group, and local partnerships abroad.
  - Ongoing development of sustainable strategies emphasizing proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used as a key client interface and know-how transfer tool.
  - Kathrein Privatbank provides wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing.
- International leasing business across CEE and Austria covering:
  - Vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers)
  - Equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries)
  - Photovoltaic plants for corporate self-use (with partners)
  - Real estate mainly in Austria via PPPs
  - Rising ESG transactions across categories, with priority on e-vehicle leasing and potential growth in e-trucks/trailers; long-term goal to increase ESG-eligible new business annually.
- Societal aspects in core business:
  - Commitment to responsible sales and marketing aligned with regulation and stakeholder expectations.
  - Strong data protection and cybersecurity practices.
  - Non-discrimination and respectful customer treatment per the RBI Code of Conduct, supported by initiatives and multi-channel access.
  - Link to broader social inclusion efforts for consumers and end-users.

nodes.title: Business on investment products
nodes.heading: Business on investment products
nodes.start_phrase: On the investment side, RBI offers advisory services for the fund and certificates business as well as for the issuance of green bonds.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of RBI’s retail and small business operations serving ~18 million customers with a broad product set (accounts, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, investment products), and Austria-specific activities via Kathrein Privatbank (investment advisory/asset management), Raiffeisen Bausparkasse (housing loans), and head office card business.
- Integration of responsible banking into retail strategy since 2023, focusing on supporting customers’ green transition, tools to understand carbon footprints, and expanding sustainability-oriented offerings.
- Commitment to grow green and social lending to private individuals and small businesses, including green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgage loans.
- Investment products business covering advisory for funds, certificates, and green bond issuance; sustainable investing largely via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft (Raiffeisen Capital Management), offering securities and real estate funds and investment management, with sales centered in Austria and extending to Italy, Germany, and CEE through local partnerships.
- Ongoing development of sustainable investment strategies grounded in proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used to transfer know-how to customers.
- Kathrein Privatbank’s services in wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing.
- International leasing across CEE and Austria in four categories: vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers), equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries), photovoltaic plants for corporate own use, and real estate (mainly Austrian PPPs); rising ESG transactions with priority on e-vehicle leasing and potential growth in e-trucks/trailers; goal to increase ESG-eligible new business annually.
- Societal aspects embedded in core business, emphasizing responsible sales and marketing, strong data protection and security, non-discrimination and respectful customer treatment per the Code of Conduct, and inclusive access to products and services across channels.

nodes.title: International leasing business
nodes.heading: International leasing business
nodes.start_phrase: There has been growth in the level of ESG transactions in all business categories and the outlook prioritizes car leasing, especially e-vehicles, in cooperation with vehicle manufacturers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope of RBI’s retail operations: serves ~18 million retail, private banking, and small-business customers with accounts, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, and investment products; in Austria, investment advisory/asset management via Kathrein Privatbank, housing loans via Raiffeisen Bausparkasse, and card business at head office.
- Integration of responsible banking since 2023: retail strategy prioritizes supporting customers’ green transition, including tools to understand carbon footprints and a broad suite of sustainability-oriented products; focus on growing green and social lending (e.g., green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgages) with targeted advice.
- Investment products and sustainable investing: advisory for funds, certificates, and green bond issuance; sustainable investment of deposits mainly via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft (Raiffeisen Capital Management) offering securities and real estate funds and investment management for institutional and private clients; primary markets Austria, Italy, Germany, and CEE; distribution via Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria and local partners; ongoing enhancement of sustainable strategies with proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used as a vehicle for client education and knowledge transfer.
- Private banking services: Kathrein Privatbank provides wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing solutions.
- International leasing business: active across CEE and Austria in four categories—vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers), equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries), photovoltaic plants for corporate own use, and real estate (mainly via PPP in Austria); increasing ESG transaction share, with strategic emphasis on e-vehicles in partnership with manufacturers and emerging potential in e-trucks/trailers; long-term goal to grow ESG-eligible new business annually.
- Societal considerations in core business: commitment to responsible sales and marketing, strict data protection and security compliance, and non-discrimination per the RBI Code of Conduct; inclusive service delivery across channels and initiatives aligned with social inclusion.

nodes.title: Societal aspects in the core business
nodes.heading: Societal aspects in the core business
nodes.start_phrase: Considering societal aspects in the core business and thus knowing and incorporating the societal needs of customers and end consumers is important to RBI.
nodes.summary:
- Scope of RBI’s retail and small-business operations: serving ~18 million customers with a broad product suite (accounts, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, and investment products). In Austria, investment advisory and asset management via Kathrein Privatbank, housing loans via Raiffeisen Bausparkasse, and card business at head office.
- Responsible banking integrated into retail strategy since 2023: focus on supporting customers’ green transition, tools to understand carbon footprints, expanded sustainability-oriented solutions, and plans to grow green and social lending (including green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgages) with targeted advisory.
- Investment products and sustainable investing: advisory on funds, certificates, and green bond issuance. Customer deposits invested sustainably largely via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. (Raiffeisen Capital Management), offering securities and real estate funds and investment management. Sales centered in Austria (via Raiffeisen Banking Group) with Italy, Germany, and CEE as key markets through local partnerships. Ongoing enhancement of sustainable strategies using proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used to transfer know-how to clients.
- Kathrein Privatbank’s offerings: wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing services.
- International leasing business across CEE and Austria: four categories—vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers), equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries), photovoltaic plants for corporate self-use (partnered), and real estate mainly via PPPs in Austria. Growth in ESG transactions across categories, with strategic priority on car leasing (especially EVs); e-trucks/trailers seen as potential growth drivers. Long-term aim to increase ESG-eligible new business volumes annually.
- Societal considerations in core business: emphasis on responsible sales and marketing, compliance with data protection and security, and non-discrimination under the RBI Code of Conduct. Delivery through various initiatives and multi-channel access, supporting fair practices and social inclusion.

nodes.title: Significant (geographical) markets
nodes.heading: Significant (geographical) markets
nodes.start_phrase: In order to achieve the maximum possible transparency and in the interest of clearer lines of reporting, segments were defined in accordance with the IFRS 8 thresholds.
nodes.summary:
- Segment definition and reporting: Operating segments follow IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center are combined and disclosed as “Austria and other.”
- Employee footprint (31/12/2024): Total headcount 43,574 across Austria and CEE. Regional totals include Central Europe 11,187; Southeastern Europe 12,455; Eastern Europe 8,852 (Russia); Ukraine 5,690; Austria 5,390. Figures cover all Group units within the IFRS consolidation scope with more than 100 employees.
- Value chain scope per ESRS: Reporting covers own operations and upstream/downstream value chains, including products/services, business relationships, and supply chain. RBI’s model centers on deposit-taking and lending to corporate and retail clients in Austria and CEE, with additional services in leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises funding sources (customer deposits, issued bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities; sustainability-related funding/liquidity risks are considered. Customer money placed in investment and pension funds is excluded. Suppliers of goods and services for RBI’s operations are included.
- Downstream value chain: Primarily on-balance financial assets (loans and leases) and investment activities. Corporate lending is the key value chain with the greatest impact materiality; retail lending is also a key element. Exposures to sovereigns, financial institutions, and central banks are not core to the sustainability-related value chain but are disclosed where market practice (e.g., PCAF) applies. A second key downstream chain is assets under management in investment and pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without such control or look-through are excluded.

nodes.title: Definition of value chain
nodes.heading: Definition of value chain
nodes.start_phrase: According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships and its supply chain.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how significant geographical markets and operating segments are defined for reporting, aligning with IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and presented as “Austria and other.”
- Provides employee headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024, covering only Group units with more than 100 employees. Regional totals include Central Europe 11,187, Southeastern Europe 12,455, Eastern Europe (Russia) 8,852, Ukraine 5,690, Austria 5,390, for a Group total of 43,574.
- Defines the value chain in line with ESRS, covering own operations plus upstream and downstream activities. Describes RBI’s business model: primarily deposit-taking and lending in Austria and CEE, with additional services in leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: funding sources (customer deposits, issued bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities; sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks are considered. Customer money in investment/pension funds is excluded from upstream. Suppliers of goods and services are included as part of upstream.
- Downstream value chain: on-balance sheet lending/leasing and financial investments that finance customers/investees and drive positive or negative sustainability outcomes. Corporate lending is the most material impact area, with retail lending also important. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank investments (primarily for liquidity) are generally not key for sustainability reporting, though disclosed where market conventions (e.g., PCAF) exist. A second downstream key chain is assets under management in investment and pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without such control or look-through are excluded.

nodes.title: Description of the upstream value chain
nodes.heading: Description of the upstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The upstream value chain of RBI consists of the financial liabilities that are borrowed as deposits or issued as bonds or equity.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and segmentation: To enhance transparency, operating segments are defined using IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and reported as “Austria and other.”
- Significant geographical markets and workforce: Employee headcount as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574 across Austria and CEE. Regional totals include Central Europe (11,187: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia), Southeastern Europe (12,455: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Romania, Serbia), Eastern Europe (8,852: Russia), plus Ukraine (5,690) and Austria (5,390). Figures cover Group units within the IFRS consolidation scope with more than 100 employees.
- Business model: RBI provides banking services to corporate and retail clients in Austria and CEE, focused on deposits and lending, and also offers leasing, asset management, pension fund business, and investment banking.
- ESRS-aligned value chain reporting: Information covers own operations and the upstream and downstream value chain, including products/services, business relationships, and supply chain.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises funding sources (deposits, bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities, with consideration of sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks. Customer investments in third-party investment and pension funds are excluded. Suppliers of goods and services for operations are also part of the upstream chain.
- Downstream value chain (financial assets): Primarily on-balance sheet lending and leasing activities. Corporate lending is the key value chain with greatest impact materiality; retail lending is an additional element. Lending to sovereigns and financial institutions and placements with central banks (mainly for liquidity) are not core to the sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market convention (e.g., PCAF) exists.
- Downstream value chain (assets under management): Includes investment and pension fund activities where RBI employees have direct operational control of the investment process. Third-party funds without such control or look-through capability are excluded.

nodes.title: Description of the downstream value chain
nodes.heading: Description of the downstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The main downstream key value chain of RBI consists of the on-balance sheet financial assets, which are lent or leased to customers and financial investment activities of RBI.
nodes.summary:
- Geographic segmentation and reporting: Operating segments are defined per IFRS 8; for the consolidated non-financial statement, “Group Corporates & Markets” and “Corporate Center” are combined as “Austria and other.”
- Workforce distribution: Headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574, spanning Austria and CEE (Central, Southeastern, Eastern Europe, including Ukraine and Russia). Data covers IFRS-consolidated units with more than 100 employees.
- Value chain scope per ESRS: Reporting covers own operations and upstream/downstream value chains linked to RBI’s banking model (corporate and retail banking in Austria and CEE), plus leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises financial liabilities (deposits, bonds, equity) used to fund customer activities, with funding/liquidity sustainability risks considered; also includes suppliers of goods and services. Customer investments in investment/pension funds are excluded from upstream.
- Downstream value chain (material focus):
  - Primary: On-balance sheet financial assets (lending/leasing and investment activities), with corporate lending having the greatest sustainability impact materiality; retail lending is also key. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank liquidity placements are not core to sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market practice (e.g., PCAF) exists.
  - Secondary: Assets under management in investment/pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without control/look-through are not key.
- Downstream activities deemed non-material/excluded: Cash and cash equivalents (mainly with central banks/financial institutions); trading assets/liabilities (short-term; climate market risk addressed under ESRS E1); non-consolidated associates and investees included only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; investment property excluded (own-use property covered under in-house ecology for climate).
- Data maturity: 2024 value chain disclosures reflect available information; broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Stakeholder engagement (SBM-2): Key groups include shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, private, SME); employees and their representatives; regulators and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, EIB, IFC, EBRD, MIGA, central banks); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society; membership organizations (e.g., WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: SBM- 2: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: RBI defines its stakeholders as those people or groups of people that have a legitimate interest in the company through their direct or indirect business activities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and exclusions in the downstream value chain: RBI deems several areas immaterial and excludes them from value chain reporting—cash and cash equivalents (mostly held at central banks/financial institutions), trading assets and liabilities (short-term; related market risk sustainability aspects addressed under ESRS E1: Climate change), non-consolidated associates and investees (only included for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; otherwise excluded from broader value chain considerations), and investment property (non-core; own-use property impacts covered in the Climate change chapter/in-house ecology).
- Data availability and roadmap: 2024 value chain information is limited to data readily accessible to RBI, with an expectation of broader coverage as CSRD implementation advances.
- Stakeholder engagement (SBM-2): Defines stakeholders as parties with a legitimate interest through direct or indirect business activity and identifies priority groups:
  - Shareholders/owners (private and institutional investors)
  - Customers (corporate, private/consumer, SMEs)
  - Employees and their representatives (unions, staff council; full-time, part-time, contractors)
  - Regulatory and supranational authorities (e.g., ECB, central banks, MIGA, EIB, IFC, EBRD)
  - Business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers)
  - NGOs and civil society (including proxies for “silent stakeholders” like ecosystems, biodiversity, local communities)
  - Membership organizations (WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI)
  - RBI Sustainability Council (internal and external ESG experts)
  - External ESG expert groups (third-party consultants, advisory panels)
- Period and context: Content is part of RBI Group’s 2024 Group management report.

nodes.title: General description of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: General description of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI defines its stakeholders as those people or groups of people that have a legitimate interest in the company through their direct or indirect business activities.
nodes.summary:
- Clarifies which downstream value chain elements are deemed immaterial and excluded: cash and cash equivalents; trading assets and liabilities (short-term; sustainability risks addressed under ESRS E1: Climate change); investment property (non-core). Own-use property impacts are covered in the Climate change chapter’s in-house ecology section.
- Non-consolidated associates and investees are considered only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; they are excluded from other value chain aspects.
- For 2024, value chain information is limited to data readily accessible to RBI, with broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Defines stakeholder engagement and identifies primary stakeholder groups: shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, retail, SMEs); employees and their representatives; regulatory and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, central banks, MIGA, EIB, IFC, EBRD); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society (including proxies for ecosystems, biodiversity, and local communities); industry and membership organizations (WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.
- Emphasizes integrating stakeholder views and ESG expertise into governance and business practices.

nodes.title: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI engages with its stakeholders through various methods to ensure their interests and views are adequately considered in the company's strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- RBI engages stakeholders to incorporate their interests into strategy and business model, assess material sustainability topics, and refine sustainability management, while participating in national and international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: annual/biannual events (e.g., sustainability summits, industry ESG forums).
  - Meetings: focused sessions with partners, regulators, and customers, often monthly/as needed.
  - Advisory sessions: quarterly or project-based with external ESG experts, partners, and internal stakeholders.
  - Training: regular, year-round education on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, and sustainability strategies for employees, customers, and partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, ESG Task Force, RBI Sustainability Committee, and workforce-related committees).
  - Working groups: cross-functional/internal-external teams on ESG initiatives, climate action, and reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and transparent customer complaint channels.
- Key topics include ESG integration, sustainable finance, climate change, human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance, financial literacy, and sustainability performance.
- Organization: a decentralized engagement model where units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance, etc.) manage their own stakeholder interactions aligned to their expertise.
- Coordination: a central stakeholder dialogue database maintained by Group ESG & Sustainability consolidates inputs from all units for reporting, documentation, and monitoring.

nodes.title: Organization of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Organization of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI organizes its stakeholder engagement through a decentralized approach, where various units engage with stakeholders based on their specific areas of expertise and operational focus.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How RBI engages stakeholders to inform strategy, business model, and sustainability management, and how these engagements are organized and tracked.
- Purpose: Gather stakeholder views, assess material sustainability topics (ESG, climate, human rights, compliance), and feed results into continuous sustainability improvement; active participation in national/international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: large formal events (annual/biannual) on sustainable finance, climate change, ESG integration.
  - Meetings: targeted discussions (often monthly/as needed) with partners, regulators, customers on ESG requirements, financial literacy, sustainability initiatives.
  - Advisory sessions: one-on-one/group input (quarterly/as needed) with external ESG experts, partners, internal teams on human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance.
  - Training: regular programs year-round on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, sustainability strategies for employees, customers, partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, Task Force on ESG, RBI Sustainability Committee, workforce-related committees) for decision-making on ESG and people topics.
  - Working groups: cross-functional and external collaborations on ESG projects, climate action, sustainability reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and customer complaint channels to collect feedback and share updates on ESG, regulatory changes, performance.
- Organization model: Decentralized execution by specialized units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance), ensuring topic-relevant interactions.
- Governance and reporting: Central consolidation via a stakeholder dialogue database managed by Group ESG & Sustainability to document, monitor, and report engagement activities across the organization.

nodes.title: Purpose of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Purpose of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: The purpose of RBI’s stakeholder engagement is to ensure that the interests and views of stakeholders are adequately considered in the company’s strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Explains RBI’s purpose for stakeholder engagement: to embed stakeholder interests and views into corporate strategy and the business model.
- Details benefits of engagement: 
  - Gathers insights on sustainability, regulatory compliance, and performance.
  - Identifies and prioritizes material issues aligned with stakeholder interests.
  - Advances sustainability goals through awareness, support, and collective action.
  - Enhances transparency and accountability via open communication.
  - Fosters collaboration and partnerships to address shared challenges and share best practices.
- Describes how engagement outcomes are used:
  - Feedback is incorporated into strategy and operational practices.
  - Inputs inform initiatives in sustainability, risk management, and policy updates, helping prioritize goals.
  - Diverse perspectives support organization-wide decision-making.
  - Significant outcomes are documented and reported where feasible despite no centralized system.
  - 2024 examples include ESG risk advisory sessions with partners, Modern Slavery Statement implementation discussions, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and sustainability strategy.
- Outlines stakeholder inclusion in due diligence and materiality assessments:
  - Engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs through meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys.
  - Insights are integrated into strategic objectives and operational adjustments to align with expectations.
  - Materiality assessment guided by ESRS, with reference to GRI and UN Global Compact, ensuring alignment with supervisory and supranational stakeholder expectations.
- Emphasizes that integrating stakeholder input supports RBI’s long-term sustainability and success.

nodes.title: Consideration of stakeholder engagement outcomes
nodes.heading: Consideration of stakeholder engagement outcomes
nodes.start_phrase: RBI values the insights and feedback gathered from stakeholder engagements and integrates these outcomes into its decision-making processes, strategy and business model where feasible.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the purpose of RBI’s stakeholder engagement: to align strategy and business model with stakeholder interests by gathering insights, identifying material issues, supporting sustainability goals, enhancing transparency/accountability, and fostering collaboration and partnerships.
- Explains how engagement outcomes are used: feedback is incorporated into strategy and operations; informs initiatives in sustainability, risk management, and policies; supports inclusive decision-making; significant outcomes are documented and reported despite no centralized system.
- Provides 2024 examples: advisory sessions with business partners on ESG risks, discussions on Modern Slavery Statement implementation, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and the sustainability strategy.
- Details stakeholder inclusion in due diligence and materiality: structured engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs via meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys; insights feed into strategic objectives and operational adjustments.
- Describes the materiality assessment framework: comprehensive process guided by ESRS requirements and international standards (GRI, UN Global Compact) to reflect expectations of key stakeholders, supervisory authorities, and supranational organizations.
- Emphasizes the goal of integrating stakeholder perspectives to support RBI’s long-term sustainability and success.

nodes.title: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: For RBI, understanding the interests and views of its key stakeholders is fundamental to aligning its strategy and business model with stakeholder expectations.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose of stakeholder engagement: to incorporate stakeholder interests into RBI’s strategy and business model by gathering insights, identifying material issues, advancing sustainability goals, enhancing transparency and accountability, and fostering collaboration and partnerships.

- Use of engagement outcomes: stakeholder feedback informs strategy and operations, shapes initiatives (sustainability, risk management, policies), supports decision-making with diverse perspectives, and is documented/reported where feasible to maintain transparency.

- 2024 engagement examples: advisory sessions with business partners on ESG risks, discussions on Modern Slavery Statement implementation, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and the sustainability strategy.

- Due diligence and materiality assessment: structured engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs via meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys; material topics selected per ESRS and guided by GRI and UN Global Compact; inputs from initiatives like UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and SBTi; continuous monitoring to track evolving stakeholder interests and trends.

- Governance for ESG: a Sustainability Council of external ESG experts guides strategy on economic, environmental, and social issues and anchors stakeholder concerns in policies.

- Climate and nature strategy: alignment with UNEP FI PRB; participation in international working groups (climate adaptation targets, biodiversity, pollution, human rights) and a core group shaping guidance to 2030; hosting a biodiversity day to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence; support for clients via tailored financial products and ongoing portfolio assessments.

nodes.title: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
nodes.heading: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
nodes.start_phrase: RBI ensures that its administrative, management and supervisory bodies are informed about the views and interests of key stakeholders – including shareholders, customers, employees, regulatory and supranational authorities, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, RBI membership organizations, the RBI Sustainability Council and external ESG expert groups – regarding sustainability-related impacts through several key mechanisms:
nodes.summary:
- Human rights: RBI developed a Group Human Rights Policy in 2023 through collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights and a cross-divisional working group, signaling a structured approach to expert- and stakeholder-informed strategy. RBI is preparing a Modern Slavery Act statement with external consultants and legal experts. - Stakeholder engagement governance: Administrative, management, and supervisory bodies are kept informed of stakeholder views—from shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, membership organizations, the Sustainability Council, and external ESG experts—via:
  - Regular engagement (surveys, workshops, Sustainability Council meetings), with insights and any NGO controversies on human rights or climate/nature reported to leadership.
  - Sustainability Committee discussions of materiality and feedback findings.
  - Regular updates on material impacts, ESG performance, risks, and compliance.
  - Internal communications (newsletter, intranet, monthly briefings).
  - A dedicated Group ESG & Sustainability Management team and local officers to run proactive dialogue and integrate insights into strategy.

- Own workforce engagement: Structured exchanges with the Works Council (including monthly jour fixe), Works Council meetings in Austrian subsidiaries, biennial employee engagement surveys, CEO calls with anonymous Q&A, and fireside chats and consultation hours with People, Culture & Organization.

Participation in the UN Global Compact Human Rights Accelerator (2023) and PRB working groups (e.g., ILO Decent Work, best practice community), along with collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute, enhances due diligence for corporate customers. nodes.title: Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: Description of material impacts, risks an d opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The outcomes, including both the material topics from own operations as well as from the value chain, are shown below :
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from RBI’s 2024 Group Management Report outlining double materiality findings and the management of sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) under ESRS.
- Core outcome: Most material issues are downstream in the lending and investment portfolios and assets under management; own operations and upstream suppliers are also assessed. Annual re-evaluation planned.
- Environmental (E):
  - E1 Climate change: Negative impacts from financing high‑carbon sectors; financial risks (credit, market, transition); opportunities in green financing, sustainability‑linked products, renewable/efficiency projects, and advisory. Own operations impacts across scopes 1–3; adaptation risks to buildings, asset lifespans, and energy/procurement prices; energy sourcing choices affect footprint.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Financing can drive biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation; alignment with UNEP FI PRB and regulatory expectations emphasized.
  - E5 Circular economy: Potential positives via procurement standards and efficient IT/hardware; downstream financing in real estate, transport, and energy contributes to waste and environmental strain.
- Social (S):
  - S1 Own workforce: DEI and inclusion benefits and risks (equal pay, discrimination, whistleblowing); employee development and training; health, safety, and well‑being; social dialogue and voice; secure employment, wages, work‑life balance; data privacy protection.
  - S2 Workers in the value chain: Potential human rights risks (forced/child labor, health and safety, wages, non‑discrimination) linked to financed clients and investments.
  - S3 Affected communities: Positive impacts via sector exclusions (tobacco, gambling, defense) and governance risk checks; social financings for essential services, jobs, and SME support (including women‑owned and underserved regions).
  - S4 Consumers/end-users: Privacy, cybersecurity, and resilience; responsible marketing and access to quality information; non‑discrimination; access to products and services. Identifies positive impacts, potential harms, and financial/regulatory risks.
- Governance (G1 Business conduct):
  - Culture of integrity and ethical compliance; whistleblower protection; anti‑corruption and bribery prevention/training; incidents risks; AML/CFT effectiveness; political engagement for informed policymaking; fair supplier relationships and ESG standards in procurement.
- Strategic linkages: Each topic mapped to business model responses (customer centricity, sustained growth, strong risk governance, efficiency), value chain segment (own operations, upstream, downstream), stakeholders, and time horizons.
- IRO management and methodology:
  - First ESRS‑aligned double materiality assessment conducted via workshops (Sep 2023–Jun 2024), separately for own operations and value chain, using ESRS 1 AR 16 touchpoints plus company‑specific topics.
  - Internal experts (compliance, data security, people & culture, facility management, procurement, risk, sustainable finance, subsidiaries, staff council, etc.) and ongoing external engagement (e.g., UNEP FI PRB working groups, ESG monitoring).
  - CSRD implementation team (finance and sustainability) led the process; subsidiaries perform aligned CSRD reporting.

nodes.title: Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: IRO-1 : Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: In the consolidated non-financial statement, RBI addresses the sustainability topics that have been identified within RBI as material, that reflect the expectations of the stakeholders, and that represented the focus of its engagement.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Impact, Risk, and Opportunity (IRO) management under IRO-1, detailing RBI’s process to identify and assess material sustainability topics for its consolidated non-financial statement.
- Methodology: A double materiality assessment aligned with ESRS, covering both impacts (positive/negative) and related risks and opportunities across RBI’s own operations and its value chain.
- Scope and timing: First ESRS-compliant assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024; processes run at Group level and by EU subsidiaries that publish their own CSRD reports.
- Stakeholder involvement: Internal topic experts assessed direct impacts; external stakeholders engaged through long-standing channels such as PRB working groups; continuous ESG topic monitoring informs materiality.
- ESRS touchpoints (own operations): Initial topic list based on ESRS 1 AR 16 and expanded with company-specific topics—10 total (5 environmental, 4 social, 1 governance), including sub-topics and sub-sub-topics.
- Process steps: Internal workshops to introduce ESRS and double materiality; experts reviewed and adapted topic lists; potentially significant topics were completed with department input; topics without identified touchpoints were deemed not material and documented.
- Responsible functions: Materiality analysis led by internal stakeholders across areas including Compliance; Corporate Citizenship/Donations/Volunteering; Data Security/Risk Management/GDPR; Financial Inclusion/Literacy; People, Culture and Organization; In-house Ecology/Facility Management; Lobbying/Political Engagement/Marketing; Procurement/Supply Chain; Risk Controlling; Selected Subsidiaries; Staff Council/Employee Representatives; and Sustainable Finance.
- Governance: The CSRD implementation project team—combining finance and sustainability experts—held primary responsibility for conducting the double materiality assessment.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The initial assessment for own operations was based on the list of potentially material topics according to ESRS 1 AR 16 data points and was expanded by adding company-specific topics.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: RBI’s process for identifying and assessing material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) for sustainability disclosure, aligned with ESRS and the double materiality principle.
- Scope of disclosure: Covers topics with significant positive/negative impacts from RBI’s operations, products, services, and value chain, and the related risks and opportunities to RBI.
- Methodology: A double materiality assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024, performed separately for own operations and the value chain.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal topic experts evaluated direct impacts; external stakeholders engaged through ongoing channels such as PRB working groups; continuous ESG topic monitoring influences materiality.
- Organizational coverage: Assessment conducted at RBI Group level and by EU subsidiary banks, which publish their own CSRD reports.
- ESRS touchpoints for own operations: Initial topic set based on ESRS 1 AR 16 data points, expanded with company-specific issues, covering 10 topics (five environmental, four social, one governance) including sub-topics.
- Workshop process: Internal stakeholders were briefed on ESRS and double materiality, reviewed and refined the list of potentially material topics; topics without identified touchpoints were deemed not material and documented.
- Internal responsibilities: Materiality analysis driven by ESG-experienced stakeholders across functions including Compliance, Data Security/Risk/GDPR, Sustainable Finance, Procurement/Supply Chain, People & Culture, Facility Management, Risk Controlling, Corporate Citizenship, Marketing/Lobbying, Financial Inclusion/Literacy, Staff Council, and selected subsidiaries.
- Governance: The CSRD implementation project team, combining finance and sustainability experts, held primary responsibility for executing the double materiality assessment.

nodes.title: Benchmark analysis
nodes.heading: Benchmark analysis
nodes.start_phrase: A benchmark analysis was also conducted, examining sustainability information (websites, non-financial statements) from nine European banks of comparable size regarding their engagement with these topics.
nodes.summary:
- Conducted a benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine similarly sized European banks to map touchpoints and identify sectoral impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Piloted AI in ESG decision-making using a language model to analyze public internal and external sources under the CSRD framework (RBI and five EU subsidiaries); combined AI with expert input to validate the internal double materiality assessment.
- Ran assessment workshops introducing the ESRS double materiality methodology, explaining evaluation criteria and scales for impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Applied a four-point severity scale (scale, scope, irremediability, probability) and a four-point likelihood scale across risks, opportunities, and potential impacts; treated potential human rights impacts as inherently likely per ESRS 1 para 48.
- Defined financial materiality as sustainability matters that cause or are expected to cause significant financial effects, considering resource continuity, relationship dependencies, and drivers of future value; set time horizons and assessed probabilities for risks and opportunities.
- Evaluated ESRS topics for positive/negative, actual/potential impacts, assessing origin (direct/indirect), location, time horizon, and then quantifying extent.
- Assessed portfolio impact materiality across the value chain using UNEP FI’s Impact Analysis Tool to evaluate indirect impacts aligned with ESRS.
- Segmented the portfolio by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management) and profiled by NACE sector, country of operation, exposure at default, and booking country.

nodes.title: Artificial intelligence (AI)
nodes.heading: Artificial intelligence (AI)
nodes.start_phrase: As part of a pilot project, AI was integrated into the ESG decision-making processes.
nodes.summary:
- Conducted a benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine similarly sized European banks to map additional touchpoints and identify sector-specific impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Piloted AI to support ESG decision-making: a language model analyzed publicly available internal and external sources under the CSRD framework (RBI and five EU subsidiaries), combining AI outputs with expert validation to support RBI’s internal double materiality assessment.
- Ran assessment workshops introducing ESRS-aligned double materiality methodology, including:
  - Use of four-point scales (1–4) for severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood across risks, opportunities, and potential impacts.
  - Distinction between actual versus potential impacts; evaluation of origin (direct/indirect), location, time horizon, and quantitative extent.
  - Human rights treatment per ESRS 1 para. 48: potential human rights impacts considered without likelihood scoring and assumed likely for calculation.
- Financial materiality approach: a topic is financially material if it causes or is expected to cause significant financial effects, considering resource continuity, dependency on relationships, and other value drivers; risks/opportunities assessed with defined time horizons and probability of occurrence.
- Portfolio impact materiality assessment of the value chain conducted with the UNEP FI Impact Analysis Tool (aligned with PRB and ESRS) to evaluate indirect portfolio impacts.
- Portfolio segmentation for analysis by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management), sector (NACE), country of operation, exposure at default (EAD), and booking country.

nodes.title: Assessment workshops
nodes.heading: Assessment workshops
nodes.start_phrase: In subsequent assessment workshops, the list with the touchpoints was completed with potentially significant topics in collaboration with the relevant departments or completed with company-specific matters.
nodes.summary:
- Benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine comparable European banks to identify additional touchpoints and sector-specific impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Pilot integration of AI into ESG decision-making aligned with the CSRD framework, using a language-model analysis of publicly available internal and external documents (RBI and five EU subsidiaries), combining AI outputs with expert sustainability knowledge to validate RBI’s internal double materiality assessment.
- Assessment workshops introducing the ESRS-based double materiality methodology, including evaluation criteria and scale construction; expansion of topic touchpoints with department input and company-specific matters.
- Materiality methodology:
  - Actual vs potential impacts assessed; origin (direct/indirect), location, and time horizon identified before quantitative scoring.
  - Severity measured via a four-step scale (very low to high) based on scale, scope, irremediability, and probability; likelihood also on a four-step scale for risks, opportunities, and potential impacts.
  - Human rights: potential impacts assessed like actual impacts per ESRS 1 para 48; likelihood not applied—topics involving human rights deemed likely for calculation.
  - Financial materiality determined by expected significant financial effects, considering resource use continuity, dependency on relationships, and other value drivers; time horizons defined and probabilities assessed for relevant risks and opportunities.
- Value chain impact materiality assessment performed with the UNEP FI Impact Analysis Tool (PRB-aligned) to evaluate indirect portfolio impacts against ESRS priorities.
- Portfolio segmented for analysis by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management), industry sector (NACE), country of operation, exposure at default (EAD), and booking country.

nodes.title: Impact materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Impact materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The portfolio’s impact materiality assessment was conducted using the United Nations Environment Programme – Finance Initiative (UNEP FI) Impact Analysis Tool.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines RBI’s double materiality approach under ESRS/CSRD, starting with a benchmark of nine similarly sized European banks to identify touchpoints and sectoral impacts, risks, and opportunities. It details a pilot use of AI—language-model analysis of public internal/external sources across RBI and five EU subsidiaries—combined with expert input to validate RBI’s double materiality assessment. Assessment workshops introduced ESRS methods and scoring, applying four-level scales for severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood, distinguishing actual vs. potential impacts, and treating potential human rights impacts as automatically likely per ESRS 1. Financial risks and opportunities were assessed by likelihood and magnitude over defined time horizons, with magnitude linked to downstream income dependency. For portfolio impact materiality, RBI used UNEP FI’s Impact Analysis Tool, segmenting portfolios (non-retail, retail, AUM) by sector (NACE), geography, and EAD, mapping sector/geography to ESRS sub-topics, focusing on direct impacts. Impact scores combine scale (EAD), scope (country needs), and irremediability, with a 66.7% threshold for materiality and room for qualitative adjustment. Financial materiality of value-chain risks is confirmed when the topical income dependency exceeds 10% and impact is likely; the ratio is defined as income from high-impact lending/investing over operating income plus interest and fee add-backs, with components specified (interest and fee income from NFCs, mortgages, investment/pension funds). Currently, climate change (E1) is financially material for risks, and opportunities in E1 and S3 (affected communities) are deemed financially material. The validation phase cross-checked results against GRI Financial Services and SASB financial sector standards.

nodes.title: Financial materiality from risks in the value chain
nodes.heading: Financial materiality from risks in the value chain
nodes.start_phrase: According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships, and its supply chain.
nodes.summary:
- Uses UNEP FI sector and geographic mappings to link portfolio exposures to ESRS sub-topics, focusing on direct impacts to clarify immediate portfolio effects while acknowledging the ESRS indirect impact perspective.
- Applies a three-part impact methodology:
  - Scale: monetary exposure (EAD) of sectors affecting ESRS sub-topics.
  - Scope: adjusts for country-specific needs to reflect geographic relevance.
  - Irremediability: qualitative assessment of reversibility/permanence of impacts.
- Combines these measures into an overall impact score per ESRS sub-topic, applies a 66.7% materiality threshold, and allows qualitative adjustments (e.g., stakeholder input) for a holistic view.
- Assesses financial materiality of risks across own operations and the value chain based on likelihood (legislation, reputation) and magnitude via income dependency of the downstream value chain.
- Defines income dependency ratio as income from high-impact lending/investing divided by operating income plus add-back of interest and fee expenses; considers >10% plus likely impact as confirming financial materiality.
- Specifies income sources counted as high-impact: interest from non-financial corporations, retail mortgages; fees/commissions from non-financial corporations and investment/pension funds.
- Concludes that financial materiality in the value chain currently applies to ESRS E1 Climate change.
- Identifies financially material opportunities in E1 Climate change and S3 Affected communities, emphasizing integration of sustainable business into core operations.
- Validates the double materiality assessment by benchmarking preliminary results against GRI Financial Services Sector Standard and SASB standards (asset management & custody, commercial banks, consumer finance, mortgage finance).
- Context: Part of RBI’s CSRD implementation and Group management report for Financial Year 2024.

nodes.title: Financial materiality from opportunities in the value chain
nodes.heading: Financial materiality from opportunities in the value chain
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the importance of sustainable business within the ESRS standard E1 – Climate change and S3 – Affected communities, it can be seen that business opportunities are identified as financially material for RBI.
nodes.summary:
- Uses UNEP FI sector and geographic mappings to link portfolio exposures to ESRS sub-topics, showing how industries affect impact areas and adding country-specific needs to prioritize topics regionally.
- Focuses the impact analysis on direct impacts for clearer insight, while remaining aligned with ESRS guidance on impact materiality.
- Applies a three-part impact scoring framework:
  - Scale: monetary exposure (EAD) of sectors tied to ESRS sub-topics via UNEP FI impact areas.
  - Scope: adjusts for country relevance based on regional needs.
  - Irremediability: qualitative assessment of reversibility/permanence of impacts.
- Combines scale, scope, and irremediability into an overall impact score per ESRS sub-topic; uses a 66.7% threshold to determine material topics; allows qualitative adjustments (e.g., stakeholder feedback) for a holistic view.
- Assesses financial materiality of risks across own operations and the upstream/downstream value chain based on likelihood (e.g., legislation, reputation) and magnitude via an income dependency ratio.
- Defines income dependency ratio as income from high-impact lending/investing divided by operating income plus add-back of interest and fee expenses; high-impact income includes:
  - Interest income from non-financial corporations
  - Interest income from retail mortgage loans
  - Fee and commission income from non-financial corporations
  - Fee and commission income from investment funds/pension funds
- Confirms financial materiality when income dependency for a topical standard exceeds 10% and an impact is likely; currently applies to ESRS E1 Climate change.
- Identifies financially material business opportunities related to ESRS E1 (Climate change) and S3 (Affected communities), underscoring the need to integrate sustainable practices into core operations.
- Validates double materiality results by benchmarking against GRI Financial Services Sector Standard and SASB financial sector standards (asset management & custody, commercial banks, consumer finance, mortgage finance).

nodes.title: Validation of double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Validation of double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: At the beginning of the validation process, the preliminary results were compared by the CSRD implementation project team against sector-specific criteria outlined in the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB).
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines a methodology that maps portfolio sectors and geographies to ESRS sub-topics using UNEP FI sector-impact and country-needs mappings. It prioritizes direct impacts for clarity, while acknowledging ESRS’s focus on both actual and potential (direct and indirect) impacts, and frames the overall analysis as indirect from RBI’s perspective.
- Impact scoring combines three measures: scale (EAD exposure linked to ESRS sub-topics via UNEP FI impact areas), scope (geographic relevance based on country needs), and irremediability (difficulty of reversing impacts). These produce an overall score per ESRS sub-topic.
- A materiality threshold of 66.7% determines which ESRS topics are material; scores can be adjusted with qualitative inputs such as stakeholder feedback for a more holistic view.
- Financial materiality of risks in the value chain is assessed via likelihood (legislation, reputation) and magnitude, with magnitude proxied by income dependency on high-impact lending/investing. The defined income dependency ratio uses interest and fee income from non-financial corporates, retail mortgages, and investment/pension funds; currently, financial materiality applies to ESRS E1 Climate change.
- Business opportunities linked to ESRS E1 Climate change and S3 Affected communities are deemed financially material, reinforcing the need to integrate sustainable practices into core operations.
- Validation compared preliminary results with GRI and SASB financial sector standards. An overall 0.66 threshold was set for both impact and financial materiality; topics exceeding it are included in the 2024 consolidated non-financial statement. Results were presented and recognized by governance bodies (Management Board and Audit Committee) with specified dates and summarized in SBM-3.
- Topic-specific disclosure on Climate change (own operations): impact materiality focuses on absolute scope 1–3 GHG emissions from energy use and business travel, recognizing global impacts without regional limits. While financed emissions are larger, own-operations impacts and mitigation (renewables, energy efficiency) are considered.
- Financial materiality for own operations covers physical, regulatory, and reputational risks. Physical risks (e.g., natural disasters, increased cooling needs) are mitigated via site selection, insurance, continuous monitoring, and energy-efficiency measures. Risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets or are flagged by stakeholders; risk management combines top-down and bottom-up approaches.
- RBI aligns with the Paris Agreement by reducing emissions and supporting renewables. Using SBTi methodology, group targets for own operations were recalculated to a 1.5°C pathway, with 2024 set as the new base year due to scope expansion and more data points.
- Operational opportunities include KPI-driven steering of business travel and energy use, reputational benefits, increased resilience, and collaboration and investment in energy efficiency to support the broader transition to a sustainable economy.

nodes.title: Impact materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Impact materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: In terms of RBI’s own operations, the double materiality principle means understanding and taking into account the impact of a company’s own activities on the environment and the impacts of environmental issues for the respective company.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and thresholds: The CFO-led operational Steering Committee presented the double materiality assessment, setting a uniform threshold of 0.66 for both impact and financial materiality; ESRS topics exceeding this were deemed material and included in RBI’s 2024 consolidated non-financial statement.
- Oversight and approvals: Direct and indirect double materiality assessments were presented and acknowledged by the Management Board (23 Jan 2024) and the Audit Committee (20 Feb 2024), with a further Management Board update on 16 Apr 2024; results are summarized in SBM-3.
- Topic-specific focus: Climate change—Own operations.
- Impact materiality (inside-out): Emphasis on absolute GHG emissions (Scopes 1–3) from energy use and business travel; negative climate impacts are recognized without regional limitation; mitigation through renewable energy and energy efficiency, with acknowledgment that financed emissions are larger but own operations remain material.
- Financial materiality (outside-in): Identification of physical, regulatory, and reputational risks linked to climate change and companies’ inaction; examples include natural disasters affecting assets, managed via location choices and insurance as part of adaptation.
- Risk management approach: Continuous monitoring, specialist input, and a combined bottom-up/top-down model; risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets (notably energy consumption) or are flagged by stakeholders; measures include energy efficiency upgrades and building improvements.
- Costs and resilience: Anticipation of higher operating costs from physical climate impacts (e.g., cooling needs) and actions to enhance resilience and reduce reputational risk.
- Targets and methodologies: Use of SBTi methodology in 2024 to recalibrate own-operations targets aligned with a 1.5°C pathway under CSRD; 2024 set as the new base year due to expanded consolidation scope and more comprehensive CO2 data.
- Opportunities: KPI-driven steering of business travel and energy use, support for renewable energy, R&D collaborations, and investments in energy efficiency to aid the broader sustainability transition.

nodes.title: Financial materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Financial materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The risks of operational activities are closely related to the environmental concerns set out to be managed in the CSRD.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and thresholding of double materiality: An operational Steering Committee led by the CFO set a unified threshold of 0.66 for impact and financial materiality. ESRS topics exceeding this level are deemed material and included in the 2024 consolidated non-financial statement. The process and results (direct and indirect assessments) were presented to and recognized by the Management Board (Jan 23, 2024), the Audit Committee (Feb 20, 2024), with a further update on Apr 16, 2024. Outcomes are summarized in SBM-3.

- Climate change – own operations:
  - Impact materiality: Primary indicator is absolute GHG emissions (Scopes 1–3) from activities like energy use and business travel. While financed emissions are larger and prioritized, own-operations impacts are globally relevant with no regional limitation. Mitigation includes renewable energy adoption and energy efficiency.
  - Financial materiality: Outside-in risks include physical, regulatory, and reputational dimensions. Physical risks (e.g., natural disasters, higher cooling needs) are mitigated via site selection, insurance, and efficiency measures. Risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets (notably energy) or stakeholders deem them material. Management uses continuous monitoring, specialist input, and a combined bottom-up/top-down approach. Opportunities include KPI-based steering (travel, energy), stronger resilience, reputational benefits, R&D collaborations, and efficiency investments.
  - Targets and alignment: RBI contributes to Paris Agreement goals; in 2024 it recalculated group operational targets using the SBTi methodology to align with a 1.5°C pathway under CSRD. 2024 is the new base year due to expanded scope and improved data coverage.

- Value chain and risk assessment framework:
  - Complement to portfolio impact analysis: Alongside the UNEP FI tool (inside-out), RBI implemented an annual outside-in climate and environmental risk assessment per ECB guidance to gauge severity across time horizons via transmission channels.
  - Multi-dimensional assessment covers: (1) risk drivers (physical, transition, other environmental), (2) transmission across risk types (credit, market, operational, liquidity), and (3) impacts under multiple transition scenarios (linked to climate stress testing).

- Transition risk and transmission channels (per BCBS):
  - Credit risk: For corporates, scenario inputs (carbon tax, ETS costs) feed sector forecasts and borrower financials to project PDs; for retail, higher energy costs and inflation increase burdens. Materiality reflects lower profitability, asset devaluations, and reduced household wealth.
  - Market risk: Policy, technology, and sentiment shifts can reprice assets and increase volatility; commodity markets—especially fossil fuels—are exposed. Correlation breakdowns may weaken hedging effectiveness.

nodes.title: Assessment of the materiality of climate and environment-related risk
nodes.heading: Assessment of the materiality of climate and environment-related risk
nodes.start_phrase: To complement the impact analysis performed using the UNEP FI Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool (s ee chapter Impact materiality assessment and in line with the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks (expectations 7.2 and 7.31), an extended annual risk assessment for climate and environmental risk drivers has been implemented within RBI’s risk framework.
nodes.summary:
- Describes RBI’s extended annual materiality assessment of climate and environmental risks, integrated into its risk framework and aligned with ECB guidance (expectations 7.2 and 7.31), complementing the UNEP FI Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool.
- Focuses on the outside-in perspective (how climate and environmental risks affect the bank’s risk profile), distinguishing it from the inside-out perspective addressed elsewhere (financed emissions, science-based targets).
- Uses a multi-dimensional approach across different time horizons that:
  - Assesses individual risk drivers: transition risk, physical risk, and other environmental risks.
  - Evaluates transmission channels into key risk types (credit, market, operational, liquidity).
  - Applies different transition risk scenarios linked to climate stress testing.
- Defines transition risk and its drivers (policy/regulation, technology, market and customer sentiment) and adopts transmission channels consistent with BCBS guidance (April 2021).
- Credit risk: explains income and wealth effects on borrowers; for corporates, incorporates macro and climate factors (e.g., carbon tax, ETS costs) to build sector-specific forecasts that feed into borrower financial metrics and RBI rating models to simulate PD under scenarios; for retail, considers energy costs and inflation burdens; materiality reflects lower corporate profitability, asset devaluations, and reduced household wealth.
- Market risk: outlines how policy/technology/sentiment shifts can reprice assets, trigger negative shocks and volatility, affect commodity markets (notably fossil fuels), and break down asset correlations, weakening hedging effectiveness.

nodes.title: Transition risk
nodes.heading: Transition risk
nodes.start_phrase: With transition risk being defined as the risks related to the process of adjustment towards a low-carbon economy, the transition risk drivers represent climate-related changes that could generate, increase or reduce transition risks.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes an extended, annual climate and environmental risk materiality assessment within RBI’s risk framework, aligned with the ECB Guide (expectations 7.2 and 7.31), to complement UNEP FI’s Portfolio Impact Analysis by focusing on the “outside-in” perspective (how risks affect the bank).
- Uses a multi-dimensional approach across time horizons that:
  - Assesses individual climate and environmental risk drivers (physical, transition, other environmental).
  - Traces impacts through transmission channels for each risk type (credit, market, operational, liquidity).
  - Evaluates outcomes under different transition risk scenarios and links to climate stress testing.
- Defines transition risk and its drivers (policy/regulatory changes, technological shifts, market and customer sentiment) and adopts BCBS (April 2021) transmission-channel taxonomy.
- Credit risk transmission:
  - Explains income and wealth effects on borrowers and collateral.
  - For corporates, models sector-specific impacts of factors like carbon taxes and ETS on financial metrics, feeding PD projections in rating models for materiality assessments under multiple scenarios.
  - For retail, accounts for energy costs and inflation burdens; incorporates scenario analysis; considers lower corporate profitability, negative asset developments, and reduced household wealth.
- Market risk transmission:
  - Highlights potential valuation shocks and higher volatility due to transition dynamics, including impacts on commodity markets (notably fossil fuels).
  - Notes possible breakdowns in asset correlations, weakening hedge effectiveness and complicating active risk management.

nodes.title: Credit risk
nodes.heading: Credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: Credit risk increases if climate risk drivers reduce borrowers’ ability to repay and service debt (income effect) or banks’ ability to fully recover the value of a loan in the event of default (wealth effect).
nodes.summary:
- The section describes Raiffeisen Bank International’s extended annual assessment of climate and environmental risks within its risk framework, aligned with ECB expectations (7.2 and 7.31) and complementing the UNEP FI Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool.
